subsubtopic: INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since this Friday the thirteenth has brought Canadians yet another increase in the cost of living to 12.7 per cent, amounting to one of the longest spurts of double-digit inflation in Canada's history, and since the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) only last night forecast in his budget more double-digit inflation, and says that interest rates cannot come down as long as the cost of living is up, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That the Minister of Finance make an honest statement at the earliest opportunity on how this government will take the lead in fighting inflation instead of punishing Canadians.

That this House condemn the Minister of Finance and censure the Minister of National Health and Welfare for failing to provide adequate or, indeed, any assistance for our elderly, our poor or for our retired citizens.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Last night's budget leaves Canadians with a sense of helplessness and frustration in their fight against inflation, high interest rates, and the recession that we are clearly in today. There is nothing in that budget to give Canadians any hope or sense of direction toward a solution of these problems. How does the minister justify a 22 per cent increase in government spending while calling on Canadians, as a principal theme in the budget, to reduce their spending, because this deceit destroys all confidence that Canadians might have had in the budget?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am surprised that the hon. member would use the words "helplessness and frustration" because they seem to describe more accurately his performance last night than the budget. The hon. member asked me to justify an increase of outlays of 22 per cent. I do not need to, because no such increase is taking place. If the hon. member did not rig an interpretation of statistics, he would not be using that fraudulent percentage increase.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to quote from page 73 of "The Budget in More Detail," the paper tabled by the minister last night. Expenditures are shown at the level of $62,711 million in 1980-81 and up almost $14 billion to a 1981-82 figure of $76,565 million. I could send a calculator over to the other side of the House, but that is 22.1 per cent. I did not give an accurate figure, I rounded it down to 22 per cent. I again ask the minister, how he can justify a 22 per cent increase in spending when he is calling on Canadians across this country to restrain themselves, Canadians who are being forced to restrain themselves because of the high interest rates, the 50 per cent increase in energy prices brought in by this government, and a level of unemployment which is forcing people out of work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member's question shows very clearly his confusion about economic policy. All in the same breath he is complaining about an increase in the rate of growth of public expenditures when the moisture on his lips had not dried from calling for expanded expenditures last night, just half a billion dollars in one shot, in the interest of restraint. I wonder when he is going to put his two conflicting personalities under control. Is he for restraint or for greater spending?
I want to tell him that the figure of 22 per cent is not correct. He is using the National Accounts, which do not net the petroleum compensation charge and the unemployment insurance contributions. Once that is netted out, the rate of expenditure is reduced to 16.3 per cent. If he will analyse that further, he will find that, apart from public debt charges, the total dollar amount that will be spent in the year to which he refers is less than the dollar amount forecast in the budget. If he looks at his statistics even further, he will find that the rate of growth excluding public debt charges is just about on target with the budget of last October. I invite him, if he intends to participate in this debate, to stay with an honest figure and not a fraudulent 22 per cent National Accounts rigged rate of growth.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am amazed that the Minister of Finance would use the word "honest" after his display last night.
Hear, hear!

I do not know how this minister can talk about ignoring interest charges-let us look at our expenditures while ignoring interest charges. Every other Canadian in this country has to pay interest and has to pay interest which has gone up to 25 per cent because of the policies that have been followed by this government.
Hear, hear!

This budget has perpetrated a fraud on many Canadians, whether they are home owners, renters, small businessmen, farmers, pensioners, people suffering from the problem of urea formaldehyde, all of whom were led to believe that the budget would provide some response to these problems in return for the average federal energy tax of $1,400 per family per year over the next five years. Why has the minister designed a budget which is restrictive, which increases taxes, and which will force Canada more deeply into recession and more than one million Canadians out of work this winter?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the minister responsible for housing. The good people of Scarborough have it hard enough; the last thing they want is him back as mayor.

subtopic: ATTEMPTS BY MINISTER TO ASSIST HOME OWNERS
speechtext: About two weeks ago, in a document signed by the minister, he pointed out that next year thousands of home owners will be faced with an extremely difficult situation. That involved thousands, as a matter of fact over 10,000 responses. I have a copy of that response with me today and I will make it available to the hon. member.
In that letter I indicated that the government's approach to the people who were experiencing genuine difficulty would be to respond to them first. That is what we have done in the program announced last evening to assist people who need help the most. It is an effective program.
I admit it is not the $1.5 billion program that the NDP asked that we should put into the economy; it is a $350 million program. That is a major introduction, a major commitment of this government to the industry, and I predict it will result in a higher number of starts next year in this country than there were this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today is Friday the thirteenth, and there are very few Canadians who are feeling lucky. Many Canadians were looking for relief in the budget last night. They were looking for relief from inflation, high interest rates, the high cost of rolling over their mortgages into 19 per cent, 20 per cent and 21 per cent mortgages, the high cost of energy, as well as relief from the economic stagnation of the recession and the high unemployment we are facing today. It did not come. The average Canadian must continue to face the fierce attack by this government and its policies on his standard of living and on his personal budget. Every Canadian must continue to feel the emotional strain that is caused by the present great disruption.
Let us cut through the chaff and the double talk of last night's budget. What has happened to the average Canadian since this time last year? Interest rates have risen from about 13 per cent to highs this past summer in excess of 20 per cent. Those who have faced mortgage renewals have found it necessary to find $200, $300 or $400 to meet higher monthly payments, and this has caused sharp disruptions in their personal budgets. Energy prices are up 40 per cent to 50 per cent, and much of this is to provide additional federal taxes amounting to about $1,400 per family per year over the next five years. The total revenue this government is receiving from
November 13, 1981

Canadian individuals and businesses is now at its highest level as a percentage of the over-all economy since the Second World War.
This morning we were reminded again of the problems the country is facing with the announcement that we have an inflation rate of 12.7 per cent. In the budget Canadians were looking for some relief from inflation and high taxes, particularly the energy taxes which affect all Canadians, regardless of their income brackets. However, there was no relief whatsoever.
The government asks for restraint. Canadians are being forced to exercise restraint when the money is just not there in their personal pay cheques. The government is receiving new energy taxes as well as other revenues, but what is it doing with them? The government has increased its spending by 22.5 per cent this year and has raised taxes a further $1.4 billion.
Let me put that into some perspective because when we see such figures we sometimes lose track of what is happening. In the two fiscal years from 1980-81 to 1982-83, the government will increase its tax revenues by 43 per cent. That is the largest revenue increase in history. The government has said it would like restraint from Canadians. I ask Liberal members opposite, who in this country can get a 22 per cent raise? Who will be able to increase their spending by 22 per cent? What if the postal workers came to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and asked for 22 per cent more income this year? Think of the reaction that would cause in the country today. Yet the government increases its spending by 22 per cent. The government has no regard for the impact of this on the rest of the country and no regard for how this affects other people's personal budgets.
What has the government given back to Canadians in the budget? We heard the minister responsible for housing bleating today about $350 million, but hold on; only $150 million of that $350 million has been committed. It has been committed over the period September 1 of this year to March 1983, about a year and a half, and $112 million of that will be going to 15,000 rental units when we need to increase rental housing by at least 100,000 units. The balance will be going to those who are hurt the most. It will provide for about 12,000 families, when the minister's own document says 30,000 to 40,000 families will be put into such a position that they will be paying 30 per cent of their incomes on mortgage payments.
Part of the program helps these people get further and further into debt by giving the banks the authority to increase these people's debts so that they can pay the banks the interest payments. That is a totally wrong way of facing this problem because it pushes Canadians who are hurt badly by high interest rates further and further into debt. That is why it is a wrong program.
The other aspect of the program is that it only affects home owners. There is a large number of Canadians today who are spending too much of their incomes on rental housing. That is because of the problems which have been created by a continually declining level of housing starts. That level has declined for five years in a row and has resulted in a zero vacancy rate,
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
pushing rents up and putting Canadians into such a position that they are putting far too much of their money into rent as a percentage of their incomes. That problem was not addressed in the budget of last night.
We have heard much from the minister responsible for housing over the past two months. We have heard all about the great things done by the MURB program and how important it was that the government extend that program. Now the minister quietly drops it. What hypocrisy!
Canadian home owners and renters must feel very let down by this budget because for three months now the minister reponsible for housing has been saying that there would be help in the budget. But this budget has been a major disappointment. As my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and as the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) have said, for that false promise the minister responsible for housing should resign. He should go back to Scarborough, but not as the mayor; I disagree with my colleague in that respect. I do not wish that on the people of Scarborough. I think the minister should go back and bury himself in Scarborough.
I would like to address some remarks to the members of the New Democratic Party because they have called for lower mortgage rates through a subsidization of mortgage rates by people who provide mortgage money. We cannot get away from the fact that the mortgage rate for one lender will be the same for all lenders, and much of the mortgage money in Canada today comes from pension funds, from credit unions and from insurance companies. Do members of the New Democratic Party want these people to subsidize mortgage rates which are high today because of ineffective government policy? Do they want pensioners to take cuts in their pensions because of bad government policy? Do they want widows who are benefiting from insurance proceeds to subsidize these interest rates?
What about members of credit unions who today are suffering from real financial difficulties, again because of the high interest rate policy of this government? Do members of the New Democratic Party want those credit union members to subsidize interest rates? There is only one answer to that question. The New Democratic Party is holding out a gimmick. It is playing with the emotions of Canadians who are very troubled and upset at the results of the interest rate policy of this government. They know it will not work. That policy is a fraud and it is dishonest.
The problem of high interest rates can only be dealt with by a real anti-inflation program that attacks the fundamental problems of inflation. That is what the broad majority of Canadians were looking for in the budget last night. Most Canadians knew there would not be something in the budget for them, such as people who have problems with high mortgage rollovers. However, they had hoped to see some help and direction leading them out of the problems they are in today. Unfortunately, that hope has been shattered.

The Budget-Mr. Wilson

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 ask the minister's parliamentary secretary, what is in the budget that will lead to lower inflation? For the past three years the financial requirements of the government have been between $10 billion and $11 billion. They have been reduced somewhat; they are just marginally below $10 billion this year.
The minister holds out some possibility that in subsequent years they will decline further. However, it has been the same year in and year out: "Wait until next year. We are going to do it next year. We are going to reduce our requirements next year." They are sounding more and more like the Toronto Argonauts- "Wait until next year". Next year just never comes.
Let us look at what I mean by that statement. In 1968 the then minister of finance, Mr. Benson, said:
We should not delude ourselves into thinking the choice is between policies of fiscal ease to counter unemployment or policies of fiscal restraint to Fight inflation-
That was when the price index was at 4 per cent. A year later he said:
I think the message of this budget should come through loud and clear... It is intended to show that we mean business in the fight against inflation.
Inflation then had increased to 4.6 per cent. In 1972 John Turner, the then minister of finance, said:
I have had to resist a good many well-intentioned temptations lest I run the risk of firing inflation.
Inflation then was up to 4.8 per cent. A year later he said:
This budget is aimed at reducing inflationary pressures in Canada and at offsetting the effects of past inflation.
Inflation that year was 7.5 per cent. A year later:
Two digit inflation ... is simply not acceptable to this government.
Inflation that year was 10.9 per cent. Just to draw my point out directly, that was the year John Turner said he was going to make a direct attack on government spending, and government spending went up that year 28 per cent, even higher than the 22 per cent it will go up this year. That was the year of the real attack on inflation in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wrestle inflation to the ground.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As my colleague has reminded me, that is the year when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I believe in my riding, said; "We will wrestle inflation to the ground." Another former minister said that "the effort to bring the rate of inflation down will go on unceasingly". That was said by Donald Macdonald in 1976. It did come down; it was then at 7.5 per cent. He went on to say the next year:
Our first objective must be to maintain the underlying trend to lower inflation.
It was back up to 8 per cent.
We are being held back by serious unemployment and inflation and we must do all we can to deal with them.
That was said by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) in 1978. It was then up to 9 per cent. Last year at this time:
The budget is designed to ensure a steady reduction in the rate of inflation.
At that time the rate of inflation was 10 per cent. As we all know from this morning's figures, it is up to 12.7 per cent. That is what I mean when I say we need to have a commitment to deal with the problem of inflation in a fundamental way, not deal with it in gimmicks that tend to buy votes in certain parts of the country so that people will not yell about it as much as they have. That is what we have to do. That is what is sadly missing in this budget.
To add insult to injury, in the face of the $55 billion increase in energy taxes in this country, we have seen the government increase taxes further in this budget by $1.4 billion. That is totally unacceptable, totally unnecessary and totally out of keeping with the times.
Since reading the budget, I have said that I believe it was written in September before we saw the impact of the high interest rate policies on the economy of this country, before we saw inflation bring in the highest level of unemployment we have seen for a number of years, a level of unemployment which will probably go higher, and an economy that is weak from coast to coast, from industry to industry. To bring in an increase in taxes faced with that reality means that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is totally out of touch with what is going on in this country.
More Canadians' earnings will, as a result of these vast tax increases, be spent by the government, not on job-producing expenditures like automobiles, clothes and household goods which we as individuals could make much more effectively, but on less productive items that will not create more jobs. The current recession, although it has already been severely hurtful as a result of high interest rates to date, will be prolonged, causing more job loss and human suffering.
It is incredible that this budget has ignored the economic weakness in the country today. There has been no attention paid to the plight of unemployed Canadians. There are no measures to turn the economy around. We have a restrictive budget when the reverse was called for. We have no vision for the future. There is no hope for Canadians facing the loss of a job. We have high interest rates, high energy prices and widespread weakness across this country.
The budget does have some minor programs for those already in real difficulty, but Canadians do not want handouts. They want opportunities. The greatest social security program of all is a job and peace of mind that inflation will not eat away at people's savings. This budget is lacking opportunity and hope for the future.
Two or three weeks ago the Prime Minister made an incredible two-faced speech to a group of Liberal supporters in Toronto. It was truly a disgusting attempt to deceive the Canadian people in the best Liberal tradition. Let us look at it.
The Prime Minister trotted out a series of statistics which showed that Canada placed fourth in a range of measures between 1973 and 1980. He drew the conclusion that that was
November 13, 1981

a good performance. Well, it was a lousy performancce. We ranked fourth during that period when all of our competitors adjusted to not just one, but two price shocks. It was a period during which two finance ministers, John Turner and Donald Macdonald, poured money into the economy to undo some of the problems they themselves had created. That in itself ran away from those problems and created the groundwork for the high levels of inflation we are facing today. If that is performance, the Prime Minister should go in for a major overhaul. The Prime Minister either does not understand, as he is too old, too tired to learn and should quit, or he does understand and should be sacked for the odious deception he is perpetrating on the Canadian people. Canada should have been far and away number one in that study. We ran away from our problems and tried to shield ourselves from reality.
The statistics that Canadians are interested in are today's statistics. There are between 900,000 and one million people unemployed. Interest rates have ranged as high as 25 per cent this summer. It is the highest interest rate of any of the industrialized countries in the world. Canadian interest rates are currently two to three percentage points above those in the U.S. Canadian inflation rates are three to four percentage points above those in the U.S. Canada is the largest single borrower in the world, looking for handouts around the world, save one, the United States, which is ten times bigger than Canada. Our standard of living has dropped during the period 1968 to 1980 from number three to number thirteen. These are the statistics which mean something to Canadians.
The Prime Minister should get his head out of the sand and into the real world and should not mislead Canadians by using these other statistics. The Prime Minister noted three times in his speech that the government deficit caused inflation.
Let me remind the House of what the Minister of Finance and other ministers said in 1979. They criticized us because we were too preoccupied with the level of the government deficit.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), the then finance critic, talked about our doctrinaire Conservative fixation with the government's deficit. What a tragedy that this Minister of Finance did not have that same fixation, that same preoccupation with the deficit, when he came into office. If the minister had, we would not be dealing with the same high interest rates that we are facing today. Conservative members and editorial writers have been repeatedly stressing the dangers of increasing and persistent government deficits.
The Prime Minister said in his speech that the Cassandras, presumably the Conservative Party and the editorial writers, were wrong. He was right: we were wrong. We thought that interest rates might go as high as 12 to 15 per cent, not the 20 to 25 per cent range they have reached.
The Liberals have been playing with the money of Canadians as if it were monopoly money. The Prime Minister talks about the Liberal policies of compassion and caring. What double-talk! What is compassionate about policies that lead to
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
interest rates of 20 to 25 per cent and 900,000 and possibly one million people unemployed?
The mortgage rollovers have resulted in a shock to people's personal budgets of $200, $300, $400 per month, and the minister increases taxes when they should be decreased because of the economy. The Prime Minister should listen to the Cassandras, the Conservatives and others, who warned them of these disasters. The Prime Minister should remember that Cassandra, although no one liked her, was always right.
The Liberals are learning after the fact what their policies have done. They have now been forced into illogical decisions. That is economic mismanagement. There is no other word for it. The policies of the 1970s and the inappropriate response of 1981 are leading Canada into a serious recession.
The Prime Minister ends his speech by saying that this Liberal government is true to the tradition of seeking the greatest good for the greatest number. This Liberal government has made an absolute mockery of the tradition of Edward Blake, Edmund Burke, John Stuart Mill and even Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The record of the past 15 years of Liberal government must make true Liberals sick. In fact, these governments have practised time-honoured but totally discredited traditions of socialism. Most thinking Liberals are now voting Tory.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When will you speak to the budget?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This did not all happen overnight. I am coming to the budget, Mr. Speaker. The truth hurts.
It is not just the policies of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, but the policies of the previous ministers of finance, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General, when he was the minister of finance, John Turner and Donald Macdonald. It is a policy of a party which has gone rotten to the core, a party which has been buffeted from lamp post to lamp post like a drunk in a hurricane of economic disaster trying to steady himself, when the government does not have any economic base from which to start.
The lasting answer to inflation and recession is a commitment to productive economics, to establish once and for all the government's determination to devote sufficient resources to placing the Canadian economy on a firm, competitive and forward-looking footing.
There is a document in the budget called "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s." It sounds good, but let us relate that to the real world. What has economic development done in this budget? The economic development envelope in the 1980 budget for the period from 1980 to 1984 would amount to $30,023 billion. In the 1981 budget this has been reduced to $28 billion, a drop of $2 billion or 6.3 per cent. So much for the commitment to economic development.
The western development fund has been axed. Farmers will receive some benefit through the broadening of the Small Business Development Bond for which unincorporated busi-

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
nesses will be eligible, but only in a very cautious way, and only for those farmers who are in financial difficulty. There is $50 million to help the Farm Credit Corporation reduce the interest rate, again only for those farmers who are in financial distress. That $50 million is a small pittance when it is spread among all the farmers in this country.
The small business bond has been extended for a year, but it is not the same small business bond that we have known in this House. It is to be used only for those small businesses that are in financial difficulty. The small business community has lost on the trade. The small business community will also receive the benefit of an increase in the ceiling for the low tax rate for small businesses. But what the minister gives with one hand, he takes away with the other hand because he reduces the effectiveness of that increased ceiling. Again, I believe that the small business community is behind on that trade.
Another element that will hit the small business community hard is the change in the rules for the investment tax credit where only 50 per cent of the investment tax credit will be available to businesses in the year of the investment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Capital cost allowance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Capital cost allowance; thank you very much. I will tell the hon. member what I am talking about. It is incredible to me that, during a period when businesses are suffering as much as they are from reductions in cash flow because many businesses cannot get credit and must put cash up front, the Minister of Finance this year chooses to introduce a change in the tax laws that will reduce the cash flow of the small business community and other businesses. It just does not make sense.
We looked for a change in the approach that the governe-ment has taken with respect to research and development. We were looking for some fleshing out of the commitment that the government has made to increase the level of research and development spending in this country to 1.5 per cent of the national income. But there is nothing in the budget illustrating any increase in the commitment that has been sadly lacking in the actual measures that will allow the country to achieve that objective. We all know that research and industrial strategy are essential to an economic and employment policy, yet the budget has no provision for investment incentives to increase research and development. The government is only paying lip service to research, as it has done in the entire area of industrial and employment growth.
The incentives for small business companies to participate more effectively in research and development just are not there. If we are to fight the problem of long-term inflation, we must see more incentive and a more meaningful approach by the government to encourage companies to build new products and to lower their costs through developing and building the products themselves rather than buying them from companies outside Canada. This is one key to reduce the level of inflation in Canada. Instead, the environment in Canada discourages
investment in the country. It increases borrowing outside the country and the level of costs faced by the industrial community.
Next I should like to deal with the established programs funding which ties in directly with research and development. The budget pointed out that the funding of the established programs fund will decrease by about $2 billion over the next five years. It is only partly offset by tax increases to the provinces. It will lead to a decline in the quality of postsecondary education and an increase in bitterness and confrontation between the federal government and provincial governments. We do not need a decline in post-secondary education. We need an increase in the quality of post-secondary education which will lead to an improvement in our capacity to meet the research and development objectives and to meet the challenge of the high technology industry which is growing so quickly.
Another element which bothers me is that the government appears to be proposing to replace the EPF funding with grants on a per capita basis. This will lead to arbitrary decisionmaking on the part of the federal government on the basis of what it calls our national economic needs. It is a nice way of saying that father knows best-we will tell you how to run your university; we will tell you how many graduates you should have in engineering and computer science; we will tell you what courses to teach; we do not want to listen to what you understand you should have at the grass roots level to respond to the industry people in your region who are telling you what their requirements will be. The universities in the country have a better understanding of what is going on than the people in the federal government. The federal government does not have the same grasp as the universities at the grass roots to respond to pressures from people with whom they are dealing on a day to day basis.
Let us look further at the economic development strategy set out in the budget papers. For some time now the Progressive Conservative Party has been pressing to take advantage of the vast opportunities which are available in the country in major projects. We have a huge potential. I think it was in my first speech after the 1980 election that I referred to this vast potential. I asked the question whether it was opportunity or burden. If we manage the opportunity correctly, the benefits to the country will be immense. If we do not, the burden will also be immense.
In the document the minister tabled last night there is a very rosy picture of the economic development potential of the country. I should like to contrast that with the reality of the Cold Lake and the Alsands projects, projects which are on the back burner today. There is no commitment by the federal government to moving those projects ahead. There was no reference in the minister's speech to the importance of getting these projects under way. In addition, there have been two energy proposals by the federal government that are pushing 40 per cent of the drilling rigs out of the country, rigs which will be needed to meet some of the available major project potential.

I also contrast the schizophrenia of the government toward the Foreign Investment Review Agency, toward the role the National Energy Program should play, as well as toward the fight with the United States over our approach to American companies in Canada. These policies are turning off foreign investment at the same time as the program is indicating that we need large amounts of foreign investment if we are to achieve our potential. The loss of confidence has forced equipment, capital and talented people to leave the country at a time when the minister is tabling a document which indicates that there are $440 billion worth of possible major projects between now and the year 2000. I do not know how we will handle these projects with men, equipment and capital leaving the country. It just does not make sense.
There is another element which points to the schizophrenia in the government. Recently the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce referred to world product mandate; he has finally caught on. I believe I made ten speeches on this subject when we were in government. World product mandate is the ability of a Canadian company, a subsidiary of a United States company or of another foreign company, to have the total responsibility for a product line. There is one problem in Canadian companies achieving world product mandate. If the top management of the parent company, which, after all, makes the decision as to whether or not to give the mandate to the Canadian company, sees a government which appears to be opposed to the interests of foreign companies, sees a country with inflation running at 3 to 4 percentage points higher than its own country, and sees a continuation of the policies which have led to those problems, why would it give the Canadian company a world product mandate? This is a problem in achieving the economic development which we know is available to us.
Let me also contrast the document the minister tabled last night to the need for skilled people. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has shown no concern for the technical oil and gas people who are leaving the country, the enormous brain drain of people leaving the country to contribute to the Canadianization of Texas, of the Williston Basin and of Australia. Those are the concerns we have today, based on the reality of today which is not reflected in the government policies. They are different from the objectives and the goals which are set out in those economic development documents.
In this area of economic development strategy, let me caution the government to steer away from too great an involvement in the decision-making process on these major projects. Because of their size, each of them is a quasi-public enterprise and in many cases needs a government decision to permit it to go ahead. The size of the projects can lead to crowding out in the sense of pulling scarce capital away from other elements in the country. It can also lead to centralizing decisions to too great an extent so that the response to normal market forces is ignored by the decision made between management and senior government officials.
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
Let me also point out to the minister the potential imbalance that can come about in favour of these major projects, an imbalance that can lead to inflation. Because of the power of these major projects, this inflation will have an adverse effect on other industries in the country but will not have the same effect on the project itself because of its size and the particular deal that government might be prepared to enter into. We must be very careful about the inflation rate induced by these major projects. I think we have seen the best possible example of this in the last two or three years in Alberta, where inflation rates are running ahead of the rest of the country and make things very difficult for other industries trying to compete in the same marketplace.
I come to my last point on the crowding out possibility of major projects. I am not making these comments in a critical way but in a positive way to try to draw out some of the problems we may face. The capital flows that will be attracted by these major projects may tend to push up the value of the Canadian dollar. This happened in the late 1950s and for other reasons in the middle 1970s. What happens is that the value of the Canadian dollar is held up, and this forces a deterioration in the competitive position of other manufacturing companies in a different set of circumstances. That is what I mean when I say that these major projects can represent an opportunity or a burden. If we manage them properly and if we are responsive to market conditions and do not deal with the major projects in isolation from the rest of the economy, the potential of this country is tremendous.
We must take advantage of these major projects because since the last war they have been a major force in the economic development of the country. We must take advantage of them because they can lead to great technological advancement. What that means is that potentially we are exporters of this technology. One of the best examples of this is the oil sands projects. We are ahead of many other countries in what we know about oil sands technology. The government does not seem to understand that we can lose that advantage. Countries like Venezuela are anxious to import our technology, but if we start to slip and these projects do not go ahead- and one is completely stalled right now-we will lose that tremendous advantage.
We can increase our capacity and expertise in project management and this can help us throughout the world. We can upgrade the skills of Canadians in this country to meet the opportunities of the future. We can improve our balance of payments. Today we have a real problem with our balance of payments, and I want to come back to that in a minute.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we can do great things for equalizing regional development in this country because many of these projects are located in the less advantaged areas of the country.
What we have to do when we compare the real world of today to that nice-sounding potential of the future is to question the competence of the government to implement and take advantage of the policies that will be necessary if we are

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
to move ahead on economic development in the major project areas.
I made reference to the balance of payments deficit. This year the minister's papers show that the balance of payments deficit will be $9.1 billion. A year ago the current account balance of payments was about $1.6 billion. In the two or three years prior to that it had been running at a level of about $4 billion. That is a major problem the country is facing.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members opposite to a statement made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce when he was opposition finance critic. This is what he said:
In his budget the minister mentioned only in passing a deficit which deserves as much and, in fact, more attention than the government's budgetary deficit, and that is the deficit in the balance of payments of our current account of international trade.
Apart from a reference in a table of figures, there is no mention that I could find in the vast number of papers set before us last night about the importance of this problem of a $9.1 billion balance of payments deficit. I should like to ask the Minister why that is so. I think I know why he has not proposed any action to face up to this problem. It is because the balance of payments is an enormous embarrassment to him.
In a question I put in the House I made reference to the huge outflow of private capital caused by the policies of this government, capital amounting to $8.4 billion, or five times the level of the average outflow during the 1970s. When you combine the capital outflow with the current account outflow, the figure reaches $17.5 billion, or nearly $1,000 for every man, woman and child in the country. That is a major problem for Canada and a problem for all of us, Mr. Speaker. It leads to an outflow of money from the country. The Bank of Canada has told us that if money flows out of the country the bank will either keep interest rates up in order to prevent that, or arrange to attract other money into the country.
We are all suffering from this problem because of the government's policy of maintaining high interest rates. That is why we should take this more seriously. That is why we have to be so concerned about the competitive position of this country which has deteriorated severely in the past year and a half.
Let me move to other proposals in this budget which I feel should have been there in order to encourage the productive capacity of this country, but before doing so, may I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I completed my comments before lunch, I was discussing those things which I felt were necessary to lead this country to a reduction in the rate of inflation that we have today, and also to generate increased economic activity. What I want to come to next is the importance of savings and investment in this whole process.
I think that all of us feel that savings are the means by which we prepare ourselves for certain expenditures down the road, whether savings for making major expenditures while we are working, or savings which will prepare us for retirement, allowing us to retire in dignity and free from concerns about where we will be getting the money to look after our requirements. However, savings are a very important element in the economic development of our country because they do provide the money for investment and also for increasing the degree of Canadian ownership in our country.
In looking at this budget, I was concerned that there are no new incentives for Canadians to save and to invest in this country. There is no increase, as an example, in the amount of money individuals can put into a retirement savings plan or a pension fund. These were last increased in 1976. Since that time, we have had some 60 per cent to 65 per cent inflation in this country. Therefore, it is not only discouraging, not allowing individuals to set funds aside for their retirement, but it is also robbing us of the savings we will need in the country to produce the plants and equipment which will create the jobs to get us out of the economic malaise that we have today.
In his remarks the minister made some slight recognition of the importance of incentive through the lowering of the marginal personal tax rates. I applaud the minister for this, and I applaud the remark that he made in his budget speech when he stated that lower tax rates will increase incentives to work, save and invest. I only wish that previous ministers of finance had had that same attitude and had not run up the level of the tax rates in this country.
However, his other actions of giving with one hand and taking away with the other will antagonize those very same people-the creative people in Canada, the entrepreneurs, the job producers-and undermine the efforts that he wants to take to encourage them to work harder and produce more jobs in this country. I fear that the gesture he has made toward the entrepreneurs and toward encouraging initiative is little more than a public relations gesture. In the battle against inflation and against this recession we are in today, we must be encouraging the entrepreneurs, the risk-takers and the creative people to the maximum extent possible because they are the people who will create the jobs which will move us out of the recession we are in today.
The key to what I have been referring to over the past few months is productive economics and the generating of incentives to get the productive side of our economy moving.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We must improve the productive capabilities of our economy by helping people to improve themselves and to upgrade their skills through training programs. We must help
November 13, 1981

businesses to become more competitive through encouraging them to expand their research and development activities. As I said a few minutes ago, there is not enough incentive in this budget, and there was not prior to it, to generate that research and development activity.
There are some broad statements in this budget as to the importance of trade, but again, as I mentioned before, we are facing a very serious crisis in this country with the size of the balance of payments deficit we have today, and apart from a general statement toward encouraging trade there is no acknowledgement in specific budget measures which will encourage trade through export promotion, and so on, in this country.
We must also do everything we can to improve and modernize our transportation systems, because with a country the size of Canada and with the distance that Canada is from our markets it is very important that manufacturers and others in the country bring those goods to markets as cheaply and as efficiently as possible. These are the programs that will help the country produce more goods and services in a more efficient and productive way. They help private individuals and companies create jobs and they help Canadians become more efficient and more skilled in their jobs. Productive economics will lead to an increase in productivity, lower costs, and therefore lower inflation, and through lower inflation, lower interest rates. A major drop in inflation and a major drop in interest rates is what this country needs the most.
Productive economics involves two other elements to be successful. It requires a commitment to encourage the private sector, and a positive attitude to see our business succeed. It also requires an understanding by government that too much government, either through excessive government spending, as we have this year with this 22 per cent increase in government spending, or an increase in regulation, which seems to be held out by this economic development plan presented with the budget papers, will inhibit productive economics from working.
The combination of this broad package of productive economics 1 discussed just now, plus the positive attitude toward private individuals, will give Canadians a sense of direction that has been missing in recent years. That combination will give Canadians the confidence to build their businesses and create jobs and opportunities for other Canadians. This may have some of the same ring as the minister's statements last night. They are both going in the same direction, but they do it in a different sort of way.
Apart from my comments on the lack of a visible commitment to achieve some positive result today when it is needed to fight the recession we have with us and to put some of those one million people who are out of work back to work, I want to draw the attention of the House to another distinction. Liberals today prefer to set the rules and intervene heavily in the decisions of entrepeneurs and risk-takers in this country. The minister clearly indicated that in the answer to some questions last night at a press conference I attended. The
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
Conservative Party prefers to set the over-all environment, to establish the ground rules, and then encourage private individuals to get on with the job without a lot of government intervention and regulation. This is an important principle that we must establish here.
Whether the government uses grants or incentives, that method of participation is the key to whether or not we are going to succeed in the economic development of our country. Grants involve politicians and bureaucrats making decisions. They are arbitrary and they can tend to play favourites. They are slower because the whole government decision-making process by its nature is slow. It also results in more regulation at a time when the Economic Council of Canada has issued an extensive report calling for less regulation.
Let me also recall a story which was set out in a book recently about the Wall Street Journal. In 1976, sending out a questionnaire interviewing a number of key economic advisers to various presidents over the ten or 12 years prior to 1976, all of these key presidential advisers were asked what they would have done differently, in retrospect, to avoid the economic problems the United States suffered from in the two or three years leading up to 1976. There was absolutely no consistency in what the right solutions could have been, with one exception, and that one exception was that they allowed monetary policy to run wild during that period. Apart from that there was no consistency in the actions that should have been taken by the government of the United States.
The conclusion I draw from this is that if these experts did not know what should have been done to solve those problems after the fact, how can they tell us how to solve the problems before the fact? That is why I am so concerned that we not fall into the trap of having too much bureaucratic control over the economic development policies that companies should follow.
In its place I think we should encourage more incentives rather than grants; for example, having the government set the broad rules to let the businessman understand what the rules of the game are and then let the businessman go out and make his decision whether or not to take advantage of that incentive. It is a faster means of approaching problems and it provides for much freer choice. It also provides for the strengths that a series of decisions brings to the solving of problems as opposed to a concentration of decisions by politicians and bureaucrats.
Concentration of decision making, whether it is in the private sector or the public sector, or a combination, is bad, and I believe should be avoided in this country.
I do not want to dwell on this topic too long. It is an important principle and it provides a real distinction between the approach the Liberals or NDP would follow and the approach the Conservative Party would follow. But most important for us to understand here is that this is the key difference between the degree of success or lack of success that Canada will have in its industrial future.
Let me conclude my remarks today by returning to the themes from the budget, equity, restraint and renewal or growth. Having regard to equity, I ask Liberal members
12752

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Wilson
opposite what is equitable, what is fair, in a pensioner losing his savings to the ravages of inflation? I have heard the Minister of Finance say a number of times in response to why there was no tax credit in previous budgets-I am sure he would give the same answer now-that he provided an increase in the guaranteed income supplement and therefore has looked after that problem. It does not look after that problem, Mr. Speaker. It addresses the problem for about a million and a quarter Canadians, but there are another million and a quarter Canadians who have been forced to see their savings whittled away by inflation, and there is another million and a quarter Canadians living below the poverty line. That problem has not been addressed by the minister in this budget or in previous budgets.
I believe it is wrong for the Minister of Finance to take credit for introducing the increase in the guaranteed income supplement, as he did last year. The Minister of Finance should be apologizing to those pensioners who, because of the inflationary policies of this government, are having to seek assistance from the guaranteed income supplement and also for having to increase the amount which was introduced last year. That is the problem in this country. The government takes credit for giving when it should be seeking the forgiveness of the people it has placed in the position they are in.
Returning to the question of equity, what is equitable about a farmer who is forced to sell his cattle to meet the bank's requirements? What is equitable about a home owner who is in a position totally beyond his control as a result of having to find $200, $300 or $400 or more a month to meet the increase in his mortgage payments by reason of a government decision? What is equitable about a small-business man seeing his business disappear in front of his eyes because he has to pay 20 per cent or 25 per cent interest rates? There is nothing so vicious or unfair as inflation and we have had far too much of it in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The next theme in the budget is restraint. I have dwelt on this theme at some length as it relates to the huge increase in spending by the government this year, a full 22 per cent. How is it equitable for the government to ask Canadians to restrain themselves when it has increased its own spending by 22 per cent? Canadians are forced to restrain themselves because of high interest rates, high energy costs and high inflation.
The final theme of the budget is growth. Where in the budget is the growth which will lead us out of the recession we are in today? Where is the growth that will reduce the level of unemployment from approximately one million and develop the potential of the vast resources of this country? The only growth I see in this budget is the growth in government, and we have learned from sad experience that this is the wrong path for this country to follow. Canadians are looking at the budget and asking themselves where is the hope and where is
the path which will lead to a solution of the problems we face today. What is the direction the government will take? Canadians are losing pride in their country and losing faith in the future.

Mr. Speaker, this is a budget which continues the assault on every Canadian. It increases income tax for Canadians and does not offer any solutions for reducing inflation and unemployment. Each year during the next five years, every Canadian family will have to pay an energy tax of $1,400. At the same time the government intends to increase its expenditures by 22 per cent this year but there is no relief for the average Canadian.
And for this reason-

I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That all the words after the word "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this House condemns and rejects a budget which fails utterly to address or comprehend the recession facing Canada or to put any of the one million unemployed Canadians back to work, which offers no help to renters and assistance to home owners so meagre as to compel the immediate resignation of the minister responsible for housing, which provides a completely insignificant stimulus to rental housing construction, which fails to provide any relief from high energy taxes and which, while calling on Canadian businesses and individuals to show restraint, pumps up federal government expenditures by 22 per cent."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!
