subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Chair has received the motion and after consultation the Table finds it to be in order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I was in the frozen food section at a supermarket and a senior citizen who was looking at a number of packages of frozen fish fillets turned to me and said: "I wonder whether the store will let me take some of the fish fillets out of the package and buy them one by one because I do not think I want to buy the whole package right now." Mr. Speaker, as we carry on this debate, removed as we are from what is really going on in this country, we have to regain a sense of what exactly it is that this economic crisis represents for the ordinary Canadian. It is not simply a question of high rates or a crisis in investment in abstract terms, or a question of a varied series of statistics sometimes deceptively presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). We are talking about a crisis in our economy which affects Canadians in their way of life, the way they respond to each other and their hopes and aspirations for the future.
When we debate this budget we are talking about our senior citizens, for example, hundreds of thousands of whom live on less than $6,000 a year. We are talking about families, many of them new to this country, some who have been here for generations and have worked and struggled hard. These people are not the ones who the members of the Conservative Party
November 13, 1981

might call the "creative elite" of our society, but they are creative enough. They are just the ordinary working people who are paying their taxes. They are the people who have worked and struggled either on the farm or in factories, mines or mills to save their money to buy a home. They have been told this last year that they will not be able to stay in their homes. Those are the people we are talking about while we debate this budget. We are talking about the hundreds of thousands of young people who are out of work and the tens of thousands more who will be added every month as a result of this budget.
We all respond with anger and concern, but the point is that it is not simply a question of another group of people who are in some abstract way added to the ranks of those people who are are without jobs. It is a question of young people coming out of school, some of them coming out of community colleges and some of them even coming out of universities who were taught, among other things-and certainly taught by their public leaders-that this was a good country and that this was a country to which their parents, their grandparents or their great-grandparents came and worked hard. They were able to buy homes and provide. These young people were taught that they would have jobs here in Canada. When they came out of school, even those who may not be in that elite to which the Tory party refers-just ordinary people looking for the opportunity to work-they look for the challenge, the joy, the humour and the fellowship which comes from having a job. They are looking for the pride and the sense of security which comes from being able to work and at the end of the week, two weeks or a month have a pay cheque, to say with a sense of satisfaction: "I worked for that pay cheque. I can buy something with it. I can get married because I have the security of that cheque. 1 can buy a house eventually. I can save and do something with the money I am working for."
That is a noble aspiration which hundreds of thousands of our young people cannot have because we have a government which has introduced a budget which does not take into account the tragedy of unemployment. This government has made a categorical decision and said that unemployment is less important than inflation. There is a phrase in the budget, either in the additional budget papers or the shortened version the minister gave last night, which says we have to wait for a while before we can resume growth. That is almost like saying, "The disturbance you are seeing is temporary, do not adjust your sets." Two years is a long wait without a job and without training. That is a long time to look for some hope for the future based, as it is, on the phony statistics of this government.
All of us in this House have an obligation during this debate not simply to talk about all the figures as they balance out on the charts and the diagrams to which the minister referred today. He said that perhaps he will have to change his diagrams. The minister does not have to change his diagrams. The minister has to change his policies so that he can respond to what is the deepest sense in the public today. People are
The Budget-Mr. Rae
looking for leadership which responds to their deepest aspirations. Our people are looking for leadership which understands that beyond all the legalities of the provinces and the federal government there is a people out there, the Canadian people, looking for leadership. They are looking for jobs, and they are looking for a government in which they can take some pride.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All of us in public life have an obligation to respond to that quest for a sense of public purpose. I will be going into the details of the budget in a moment, but the overwhelming impact of the budget is that it is an expression of defeat and bankruptcy. The budget, in affect, says; "There is nothing we can do. We do not have solutions to your problems. We cannot deal with the problem of recession." I do not think I am giving any secrets away when I say that when we were asking the officials about the budget last night, one of them said, "I am sorry, we cannot provide you with that answer because if we do this, that will inevitably happen, and therefore we cannot do it." There is an obvious answer. If the government opposite and the officials in the department who are responding for the government cannot give the answer and cannot deal with the problem, let them move aside and let somebody else drive.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a non sequitur.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has been in office for so long he just assumes that if he cannot do it, nobody else can. We have seen the consequences, and the railway workers and railway consumers of Canada have seen the consequences, of that kind of attitude.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Another non sequitur.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me give an example of what is really happening on the streets, in homes and in the factories of this country today. The minister can read about it if he likes. If he cannot see it or finds that he cannot move around enough to feel it and touch it, he just has to read the report of the task force on job opportunities. That parliamentary task force did an excellent job. One of the astonishing facts the task force pointed out is that 4.5 million Canadians are functionally illiterate.
One would think that a government which received that kind of bombshell statement would bring in a budget which would set as a great priority seeing to it that all Canadians can read and write well and have a chance to compete in a job market which is becoming much more ruthless than the one their parents knew. Does the Minister of Finance say that there will be a full scale frontal assault on illiteracy? Does the minister commit his government to full employment? Is the minister prepared to admit that the greatest problem facing the Canadian people today is the insecurity which is brought about because workers see their fellow workers being laid off? Some workers have been in factories not for five years and not for ten years but for 15, 20 and 25 years, and they are being

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Rae
told, "Sorry, boys, the plant is closing". That is not simply a problem in the sense that unemployment means we will be producing less as a country or in the sense that we are falling behind in the competitive race with other countries-although it does mean that-but in the sense that it means tremendous personal unhappiness caused by that kind of insecurity.
1 have talked about it, my leader has talked about it and it is worth emphasizing again and again: people have assumed- because they were Canadians, dammit all, and because they were proud of themselves, their jobs and their achievements- that they would be able to buy homes and that those homes would be theirs. They made reasonable plans on the basis of interest rates of 10 per cent and 12 per cent, and some even made plans based on interest rates of 14 per cent. They felt that if both mother and father and perhaps one of the kids were working at a part-time job, they could keep their homes together.
However, we now know that we are not talking about an economic system-the Liberal-Tory economic system-that gives people that sense of security. These are the parties which believe in private property. What more fundamental attack on private property can one imagine than rates of 22 per cent, 23 per cent and 24 per cent for first morgages? Those rates are not being compensated for in this budget. Those rates were the ones of last summer; people sacrificed everything in order to hang on to their homes at 24 per cent and they are getting absolutely nothing from the Minister of Finance.
The minister has a defence. He put it forward in his budget. His defence is inflation. He says he cannot do anything because of inflation. When I first came to this House three years ago, I directed my first question to the then minister of finance, who is now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). That day interest rates had gone up from 9.5 per cent to 10.25 per cent, and at that time the rate of inflation was 8.9 per cent. He said there was nothing he could do, that the Americans were doing this, the dollar was doing that, it was impossible; the problem of inflation had to be combated and the only way to fight inflation was through high interest rates. We had an election. The Tories were very critical of that interest rate policy. They promised they would bring it to an end.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) became minister of finance and the rates went up and up and up. Four times they went up. The hon. member for Windsor West, now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), criticized, moaned and groaned as the rates went up over 14 per cent. He appeared on a television program on which I had the misfortune to appear at the same time. He said: "If the rates go over 14 per cent, I will resign." It is a pity they did not ask him the additional question: "What if you do not keep the promises on FIRA, will you resign then?" He would have said yes. He is a man of principle during an election.
The interest on the average consumer loan today stands at 21 per cent, 22 per cent and some at 24 per cent, if it was negotiated as recently as three weeks ago. Mortgage rates
hover between 19 per cent and 20 per cent. Where is inflation? Inflation is at 12.5 per cent. Inflation has gone up almost four points since I asked that first question three years ago, and interest rates have more than doubled. The policy is, quite simply, a nonsense. It is one which does not make any sense. Ask the workers in Baie Verte, Newfoundland, who have been laid off. The mines have been closed even though they were making a profit. Ask the workers in the fish plants on the south shore of Nova Scotia, the miners, paper workers and fishermen in New Brunswick, the farmers and the businessmen in Quebec, the workers at Admiral, Inco, Massey-Ferguson, Chrysler and Stelco, the beef farmers in Owen Sound, the wheat farmers in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the cattle ranchers in Alberta and the sawmill workers in British Columbia, whether the effect of high interest rates is to bring down inflation. Since the minister used this expression in the House, I think I can use it: their answer would be "Like hell".
The only thing those interest rates have done is to squeeze jobs out of the economy. The interest rate juggernaut swept across not simply Canada but all the western economy, bringing small business people to their knees, forcing thousands of plants to close in this country, making our manufacturing sector completely and totally uncompetitive in some regards, raising the price of food and products. The minister says that the interest rate policy is an integral part of their fight against inflation. The interest rate policy has jacked up inflation. The evidence is there for the minister to see.
Reducing inflation will take patience, persistence and time. The government is not going to wrestle it to the ground. Those who have to somehow prove their manhood in their verbal assaults on the mind tell us that is what they want us to do. The policy of the government on inflation is that in order to get the inflation rate down half a point or a point, they have to reduce the real economy to a desert. No doubt they will call that desert "peace" and claim victory over inflation. However, what is the cost to people, the cost to the real economy and to Canadians' sense that their economy and lives are something that they want to take pride in? Energy costs are rising by nearly 40 per cent a year. Food costs are rising dramatically because of changes in world patterns of consumption and demand. Much of our economy has ceased to be genuinely competitive because of the nature of corporate and government power. Where is their ability to administer prices? It is nonsense to suggest that the way to deal with this kind of inflation is through an interest rate policy of 20 or 25 per cent.
Those who live in poverty are not helped by this policy, they are damaged by it. Those who live on fixed incomes are not helped by this policy. Those who live on the margins of our economy who sometimes find a job and sometimes not because they do not have the skills or the training, who may be the wrong age, in the wrong class or have a disability-those people are not helped by this policy. This policy helps only a few people. It helps the wealthy savers and the banks. It benefits the banks at the expense of consumers, farmers, small-business people, home owners, and even benefits, at the
November 13, 1981

expense of the banks' own competitors, the credit unions and the caisses populaires.
There were three parts to the minister's budget. Like Gaul, it is divided into three parts. I wish the minister's gall was divided into three parts. Restraint: that is the cocktail party word for cutbacks, in case some are wondering what restraint means. It means cutbacks or hardships. Equity: the minister had nerve even referring to the concept of equity in this budget, but I will come to that in a moment. Renewal: renewal is the Liberal word for retreat. That is what this budget represents.
The minister talked about equity. Whose tax rates were reduced the most? Canadians earning over $100,000 a year. There are not many people in my riding earning that amount, but I am sure there are Canadians somewhere who earn that much money. They must be the ones who attend the dinners at which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asks for restraint. Their marginal rate is cut from 43 per cent to 34 per cent.
What about the single pensioners over 65, over half of whom in Canada are living in conditions of poverty and tremendous difficulty? What kind of tax reduction did they get? Zero. Not a cent, not a nickel, not a dime from the Minister of Finance. The minister talks about equity. Equity is a fancy lawyer's word for fairness. Where the hell is the fairness in that? Where is their fairness in giving nothing to pensioners? There is nothing at all in the budget for pensioners.
Then we have the claim of equity, where the minister says they are giving a tax break and the press even reported it as a tax credit. The minister has taken up the lingo. People are willing to believe the minister. They want to believe him. He is the Tinkerbell of Canadian politics. People want to believe Tinkerbell. If Tinkerbell says it is true, it is going to be true. If we all wish it were true, the lights will suddenly come on and all the people will go back to work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tinkerbell is a ding-a-ling.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is utterly fantastic to claim that the tax measures in this budget are in any sense an exercise in fairness. Today I read to the minister a section from his budget talking about a typical family of four being able to earn about $15,000 without paying any federal tax. The minister took some affront when I asked whether he thought it was time that the government recognized that there are women in the labour force who actually think they should be there.
Let me give an example. I see the minister of mines looking up. She is responsible for the status of women. I would like her to have a word with the minister. Let me use the example of a professional woman earning $20,000 or $25,000 a year, single, with dependent children. What is her tax break? Her tax break will be to pay an extra $146 to the government. The minister was saying that there were tax cuts for all these people earning over $11,000. What about that person? The thrust of it is that married taxpayers who have an unemployed spouse will receive some extra money; but those Canadian couples by the hundreds, thousands and millions who are married and who both work, both playing an equal role in the
The Budget-Mr. Rae
home, both playing an equal role in the marketplace, trying to get a job, hold together and pay these 20 per cent, 22 per cent and 24 per cent interest rates, what kind of tax breaks do they receive? Zero. Absolutely nothing. The minister said he would introduce an equitable budget. There is no equity.
Another example, Mr. Speaker, are the Canadians who have emigrated to this country or who have been here five, ten or fifteen years, who have a mother or father they are supporting in Greece, Portugal, Italy or Pakistan. But for all the hundreds of countries that have benefited by their contribution to the life of this country, what is the fair contribution of the Department of Finance to fairness? It says there has been a little fraud here. Instead of punishing those who have committed fraud, the department is going to eliminate the possibility of making that exemption entirely.
Let me say to the minister that there is a Greek restaurant worker in my riding whose wife works and sends $200 a month to his mother or father living in Greece. That was the purpose of their emigrating to Canada. What is the size of his tax break? He loses a $2,000 deduction. His taxes could increase by $300, $400, $500, depending on his marginal rate. That is the real effect. It is so important, Mr. Speaker, that we must come down from this sense of abstraction of deficits and balances and numbers coming from here and there. They are important; they are part of what the grim science of economics is all about. But it is time we got away and asked what is the real social effect of a budget which says to a Greek Canadian he is second-class, which says to a new Canadian he is not as good as somebody who has been here before, that they can claim an exemption for a dependant but he cannot. The reason is that there has been fraud.
If there has been fraud, then let those who are guilty be punished. Since when did we in this country ever go in for the notion of collective guilt? Since when was that an aspect of the Canadian culture we are proud of? It is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker. It is not a major money-making thing. It will not gain any terrific revenue for the government. But at a time of economic hardship I think of my constituents and the city of Toronto and of the kind of niggling attitude that is created on the streets. We are trying to create a multicultural, multiracial Canada, Mr. Speaker. There is no such thing as a second-class Canadian. We are all boat people. We are all immigrants. If there are those among us who have committed a crime, then let that person be punished. If the government wants to tighten up the regulations, then let those regulations be tightened up. But let us not abandon the very essence of the notion that if you have a dependant you are supporting, just because that dependant does not happen to live in Canada you should not be regarded as some kind of second-class Canadian.
The unfair and absurd attitude of the government's policy is what has led the NDP to move an amendment to the Conservative amendment today. It will provide some grounds for debate and add additional grounds for concerns that have not

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Rae
been entirely expressed in the Conservative motion. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent):
That all the words after "high energy taxes" be deleted and the following added thereto:
"and, further, this House condemns the government for failing to provide any tax relief or pension reform for senior citizens; any help for Canadians living in poverty, fair tax measures for working women; for abandoning completely its election promises on foreign ownership, FIR A, and industrial strategy; for failing to exercise control over our Financial institutions to ensure mortgage and interest relief; and for failing to introduce an excess profit tax on the banks."
I should like to speak to that motion in my closing remarks. We come to the third theme of the budget, renewal, the Liberal word for retreat. I remember it vividly because it was toward the dying days of an election. When one is inevitably worried and is looking at the poll results, one thinks about his future. The Prime Minister, although he was leader of the opposition for that brief, glorious period, went to Toronto and spoke to the advertisement club. The Toronto Star had a large headline-the Toronto Star is sometimes unfairly called the Trudeau star-but I am not one to describe it that way. When the Prime Minister came to town that day he talked about foreign ownership and about changes that the Liberal government would bring to industrial strategy. There were very specific promises and commitments made with respect to FIR A regarding where it would be strengthened and expanded. It would deal simply not with takeovers but would carry out a comprehensive review of the role of foreign ownership and demand that multinational companies be assessed on a continuing basis for their contribution to the Canadian economy.
In the Speech from the Throne the Liberals said that this is what they would do. It was ambiguous, to say the least. We knew the retreat was on its way. But to announce, only two seats away from the patron saint of FIRA, that FIRA was being abandoned totally, and to say that this is an exercise in renewal, means that we have a new definition of a Liberal. It is one who does not know the meaning of embarrassment or shame. I cannot believe what the minister had to say when he said that this represents a renewal of Liberal policy. Listen to this renewal: "The special measures being employed to achieve more Canadian ownership and control of the oil and gas industry are not, in the Government of Canada's view, appropriate for other sectors". Why not? There is no explanation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They do not tell us why. I will come to why. Why is zinc and nickel shipped out of this country without being refined? I am thinking of one company in northern Ontario. Why are resources such as uranium or nickel sold? A pound of uranium or a pound of nickel sold is a pound of uranium or nickel gone forever, the same as oil. They are non-renewable resources. Inco did not plant nickel in the ground and reap it every year. It has been there for generations upon generations. I know the Tories do not like the NEP, but at least they can agree that what is true for oil should, for heaven's sake, be true for other non-renewable resources. Why not? There is no
explanation. We are simply told that no legislative changes will be introduced to FIRA.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Suddenly it is good for us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) just said, suddenly foreign ownership is good for us. Walter Gordon must be rolling over in the Commerce Court Building. Canada has historically benefited to a substantial degree from the application of foreign capital to our economic life. There is no mention of Watkins, no mention of the Gray report, no mention of research and development and its impact upon secondary industry, no mention of the fact that we have become a colony in our own land with respect to many of our resources. All that has been completely and totally abandoned. That is called Liberal renewal. It is more than chutzpah. It is an unbelievable expression of disdain for the intelligence of the average Canadian person.
I suggested to the minister three weeks ago that the budget would have to do four things. It would have to provide for action on interest rates. There has been no action on interest rates of any significance whatsoever. I suggested that we had to have real tax reform and tax relief, that we had to have measures on pensions, and that we had to have meausres to guarantee a continued level of social service spending by the government. The only action on interest rates has been to provide relief, not to home owners, not to tenants, but to the banks. The banks are supposed to bleed a little, in the words of the minister. Well, the plot thickens. There is no action in this budget which does anything other than increase the financial power of the banks, increase the revenue going to the banks, increase their ability to exact and enforce contracts on individuals who are in a completely unequal bargaining situation. When George Brown walks into the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, he is not exactly looking at an oriental bazaar. He is faced with a contract. He cannot exactly haggle over the terms of the contract. It is written out and he signs on the dotted line.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take it or leave it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He takes it or leaves it. A mortgage is not a contract in the sense of a totally voluntary relationship between two people. It is something which is forced on people because of their economic situation. For the minister to talk the language of contracts, as if this were some kind of totally voluntary arrangement between two people who happen to meet in the street, is so absurd as to defy description.
The interest rate deferral scheme is a con. The interest rate deferral scheme is a fraud. It is a system of permanent debt which would be outlawed by any consumer protection legislation worthy of the name. If we had a minister of consumer and corporate affairs who was doing the job he is there to do, he would be calling in the heads of chartered banks and saying, "What is this? You expect somebody who has a $60,000 mortgage to pay $8,000, $9,000 or $10,000 per year in interest payments and at the end of the year owe $62,000! You expect
November 13, 1981

us to subsidize that and guarantee that kind of scheme! "It is unbelievable that that is the government's definition of interest rate relief. The minister said, "Well, it was recommended to me by the banks". Surprise, surprise! If the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) was recommended a scheme of gun control legislation by the Mafia, would he be obliged to accept it? According to the minister, apparently yes.
Finally, our motion calls for action on an excess profits tax on the banks. This kind of well-meaning but hopeless volunteer-ism expressed in the budget speech of the minister is so pathetic as to defy description. Let us listen to what he said. One would think he was just some guy expressing an opinion, rather than the Minister of Finance of the Government of Canada. He said, "I want financial institutions, especially banks, to do more." Also he said, "I particularly want them to ensure that ample funds will be available to smaller borrowers at the lowest possible margin of cost over the rates which they pay to their depositors." Where has the minister been for the last 15, 20 or 25 years? What kind of well-meaning rotarian expression is this-"I want financial institutions, especially banks, to do more?"

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the minister wants the banks to do more, he has the means to do it. He does not have to get down on his knees in the House of Commons and ask in supplication for the financial institutions to bleed a little. What a pathetic statement of defeat! I think Canadians were expecting something a little different and a little better from the minister. He is somebody who has a long history of contribution to the country. He is somebody who comes from an area for which I know he has a deep feeling. I can only say to the minister that I am disappointed-not surprised-that he, his government and all supporters of the Liberal party on the other side, have become captives of an abstract economic theory. This theory bears no relationship to people. It hurts the average Canadian. It punishes the average Canadian. It provides a statement which will only lead to even greater hardship in the months and years ahead.
I said the minister was Tinkerbell. I meant that semi-seriously, because if we look at the end of the budget speech we will see:
The key which can open the door to our future is a change in our attitudes and expectations.
All I can say is that that is a Tinkerbell kind of statement- if we all get together and really believe that inflation will come down, that jobs will be created tomorrow, or that interest rates will come down, if we close our eyes and wish ever so fervently, then it will happen; if we all wish that the banks just charge a little lower interest rate and give a break to small-business men, then magically it will happen. That is what I call Tinkerbell economics and Tinkerbell politics. It is a rejection of the deepest, most serious and most joyful aspiration of Canadians for an economy which is working, fully employed and truly fair, which takes care of all its citizens, however badly off they are, whatever colour or race they are, from
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove
wherever they come in the world. That is the vision the New Democratic Party is proud to offer to Parliament and to Canadian people. Those are the practical policies and the policies which follow from them that we will be putting forward when we are the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words in this debate are to congratulate my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), on the measures which he has proposed in response to the economic circumstances in which the country finds itself today.
I wholeheartedly support his sensitive and sensible approach to the restoration of our national economic and financial well-being.
I particularly appreciate the minister's response to the problem which, as hon. members know, has recently absorbed so much of my time, energy and concern. I mean, of course, the assistance that will now be provided through the Canada mortgage renewal plan to those Canadians who are having the greatest difficulty in meeting their mortgage payments because of high interest rates which they must pay on renewal. These problems arise, not only because of the high rates but because the rates have risen so quickly, giving little opportunity for families to make the necessary adjustments in their household budgets. The mortgage renewal plan will give them the time they need to work out their own solutions.
I am most grateful, Mr. Speaker, to the many friends, in this House and outside it, who have expressed their concern about the unprecedented amount of public attention which has been directed toward me and my portfolio during recent months. As the minister reporting to Parliament for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I have been, quite naturally, the focus of feelings of anger and frustration among people who were in fear of losing their homes. Throughout that time, I have repeatedly given assurances that the government would abide by the commitment made in the throne speech, that we would, in the words of the speech, "-act to assist those unable to bear the burden of renegotiating their home mortgages in the present abnormal situation so that the spectre of foreclosure will be avoided."
I would ask hon. members to witness that my confidence in the Minister of Finance and my cabinet colleagues has been justified. We have kept the faith; we have kept that promise.
We have done exactly what we said we would do, and we have done it exactly as we said we would, by directing assistance to those most urgently in need of it and, again in the words of the throne speech, "-without the government embarking upon a major subsidy program."

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove
I have been asked many times in recent weeks, and so have my colleagues, who are the people most in need of help, how will they be defined? The answer is now quite clear. Householders in need of help are all those who have to renew their mortgage at a rate that will take up an excessive proportion of their gross incomes. We are saying that an "excessive proportion of income" will be more than 30 per cent, paid out in mortgage principal, interest, and property taxes, with some allowance for condominium fees, where they apply.
These are Canadians who, because of the present level of interest rates, and their recent rapid escalation, will be faced with the necessity of making significant adjustments in their personal financial arrangements during the next year.
There has been a great deal of speculation as to how many households would be included in this category over the next 12 months.
Much depends, of course, upon what will actually happen to the level of mortgage interest rates. These remain painfully high, but have dropped considerably during the last month. Our estimates indicate that if mortgage interest rates over the next months were in the 20 per cent range there would be something, as I indicated this morning, in the order of 50,000 householders between now and a year hence for whom mortgage payments and taxes after renewal would represent more than 30 per cent of gross income. The great majority of these householders will have some equity in their home.
People who have a substantial equity in their home can make use of that resource to help themselves through this period of high interest rates. Several mortgage lenders have offered to defer interest payments-to allow borrowers to postpone the payment of interest and to add it to the principal amount owing. That, of course, is not a permanent solution. As long as interest payments are being deferred, the debt is increasing and is, itself, bearing interest at a high rate. It is a way, however, that some people would choose in order to reduce their mortgage payments. But this alternative is not offered by all mortgage lenders to all of their clients. Some lenders are not prepared to accept what they consider an additional risk.
In order to reduce the risk entailed by the deferral of mortgage interest for borrowers who have equity, the government is offering a guarantee. Where the home owner has an equity of 5 per cent or more in the home but is paying out more than 30 per cent of household income in monthly payments, the government will assist to arrange the deferral of interest payments by underwriting the deferred interest.
This guarantee will make it easier for the lender to offer interest deferral, in cases where the borrower wants it, in order to reduce the amount of current mortgage payments.
The special guarantee, however, will not address an even more difficult problem for other Canadians. Some of the householders whose debt service ratio will be over 30 per cent as a result of renewal, will have insufficient equity in their home. Interest deferral does not answer the problem faced by these householders who need it most. To increase their mortgage debt beyond reasonable limits would, in all probability, simply add to their problems in the future. For these householders we intend therefore to make grants in order to keep their monthly payments within manageable limits.
That, in essence, is the Canada mortgage renewal plan-a system of interest-deferral guarantees and grants. It is available to people who would be paying more than 30 per cent of income in monthly payments after renewing their mortgage. For people who have substantial equity, there is help in making an interest-deferral arrangement. For people who have less than 5 per cent equity, there are grants to bring their mortgage payments to a manageable level. The plan will be in effect for one year until November 12, 1982. It will be retroactive, applying to mortgages that matured on or after September 1, 1981. There is a limit of $3,000 per household, over the next 12 months, on the amount of interest deferral subject to the special guarantee, or on the amount of grant.
I should perhaps say a special word here about a group of home owners in which the government has a special interest, those who bought homes under the Assisted Home Ownership Program.
There are two types of AHOP participants. The first are people who receive outright grants. For these people, in order to bring them parallel to the plan announced last evening by the minister, the AHOP grants will be increased to a maximum of $3,000.
The other people are AHOP borrowers who received interest-reduction loans rather than outright grants. These people will be eligible for either deferral plan guarantees or the grant under the Canada mortgage renewal plan.
In the past few weeks and months I have met with many individuals and organizations to hear their representations and to seek practical solutions to the mortgage renewal problem. I have met with hundreds of home owners in Ottawa and different parts of the country, including the large delegation which assembled on Parliament Hill, and with my own constituents. I have met also with organizations of builders and lenders and representatives of the real estate industry.
I am appreciative of all these offers of advice. After much serious deliberation, the government has chosen a plan which is precisely targeted to people's needs and which does not put an excessive demand on public resources in a time of economic restraint.
The mortgage renewal aid measures will be given effect through necessary amendments to the National Housing Act which I will put before the House at the first opportunity. I am confident, given the urgency of the situation which the legislation addresses and the concern expressed in this House for the plight of home owners, that it will be dealt with expeditiously by hon. members on all sides.
In the meantime, the Minister of Finance will be reminding the mortgage lenders that the plan is retroactive and will apply to any arrangements they have made with borrowers during
November 13, 1981

the interim. In addition, officials of CMHC will be meeting on Monday with the lenders to discuss procedures and to enlist their co-operation. All of these measures are confined to home owners who are now renewing their mortgages or who will be doing this during the next 12 months.
I would not like to give the impression that mortgage renewals are the only difficulties facing the housing sector. There is a growing awareness of the needs of people who rent their homes and who, in many parts of the country, are having difficulty finding suitable accommodation at an affordable cost. In response to representations concerning this, I am very pleased that the government has made provision in the budget for interest-free loans of $7,500 a unit to assist in the construction of as many as 15,000 additional units. This would be affordable rental accommodation in areas where the shortage is most severe. About 5,000 of these would be available for low-income people through rent supplement programs which, with provincial cost-sharing, provide assistance geared to income.
I would hasten to add that these 15,000 new additional units, with a provision for low-income people, will be in addition to the 25,000 social housing units which will be supported under the popular co-operative programs that serve people of modest and low incomes. In all, when one combines them, 40,000 rental and co-operative units will provide suitable accommodation for people in the low, moderate and middle-income ranges.
In the next few weeks I intend to travel across the country to meet with provincial housing ministers regarding the application of the new rental program I have just described. A number of provincial governments have programs of their own to stimulate rental production, and provinces do participate in our existing non-profit programs. The new national program of interest-free loans is not being put forward to replace what the provinces are now doing. It is intended as an additional impetus to rental construction. It will be necessary for me to discuss the strategies with the housing ministers if we are to deploy the new rental program in the most effective way for all Canadians. At the same time, I intend to encourage the provincial ministers to complement our programs with any provincial initiatives designed to suit regional needs.
While we are concerned about measures to alleviate current problems, such as high interest rates and low vacancy rates, we should not allow ourselves to be distracted from our continuing attack on long-standing problems. I am thinking, for example, of our ongoing efforts to improve the housing conditions of native people and the rural poor. I am happy to be able to say that through our rural and native housing program we have been able to make very substantial improvements in the conditions of these Canadians in recent years, while attempting to assist them to achieve economic and social development. This program has been evaluated with the direct participation of the native people themselves. I hope that I will soon be in a position to propose innovations which will make the program more effective, efficient and equitable for all the people it serves. Improvement in this particular program has a high personal priority for me.
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove
I would like to remind all hon. members that housing for some 400,000 households in Canada, almost 5 per cent of the existing housing stock, is provided in different ways by the national government under programs such as public housing, co-operative and non-profit housing. This includes housing for the elderly and for women raising families alone who could not otherwise afford to obtain suitable accommodation without depriving themselves or their families of other necessities.
There are, however, some limitations to the existing social housing programs of which I speak. Not everyone has access to the limited stock of social housing. Most of the housing provided through this technique is new, and consequently adds to the stock. That is an important advantage. However, the disadvantage is that it also adds to the difficulties of generating a sufficient supply of housing. If we relied only on this technique, it certainly would require a long time and costly expenditure to serve the needs of Canadians.
For these reasons, as many hon. members are aware, I have been turning my attention to additional ways of providing housing for people who are not able to fend for themselves. One approach is the idea of shelter allowances, giving people money to seek out their own accommodation in the market, rather than putting them into special, subsidized units. The idea is to provide assistance to people rather than to buildings. I have raised this idea on a number of public occasions; most recently, at the all-sector housing conference in March of this year. I have raised the idea with the ministers for housing in the provinces at our meeting in June.
There are many aspects to this system which require and are receiving further study, such as the effect of shelter allowances on rents, the question of quality standards, limits on unit prices, and many more. Overriding all other considerations, of course, is the question of cost during a period of serious economic constraint. Nevertheless, I intend to continue discussions with the provincial housing ministers on this subject. It is a matter which I am continuing to discuss with my cabinet colleagues, especially those with responsibility in the area of social programs.
I would like to speak for a moment about Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. CMHC is, of course, the agency through which all of this assistance is delivered. Its staff has a continuing role, not only in implementing government programs, but in helping to select and develop new measures, as we did recently. CMHC will, of course, act in the government's behalf in administering the mortgage renewal plan, as well as many other forms of assistance under the National Housing Act. I think it has been well recognized for some time that CMHC has been doing an excellent job, even though it has had to operate within a legislative and regulatory framework which has often imposed serious restraints on the way in which it does business.
As I have mentioned, I intend shortly to introduce amendments to the National Housing Act to authorize the mortgage renewal plan. At the same time, I will take the opportunity to propose other amendments which will assist first time home buyers by making possible more flexible mortgage instru-

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove
ments, and will assist builders of rental housing by permitting higher loan levels. The mortgage renewal plan and the rental stimulus program that I have talked about today are addressed, of course, to the present problems arising from mortgage interest rates.
There are, as I have indicated, other problems associated with high interest levels. The treatment of these problems requires new mortgage lending techniques to which the present National Housing Act is ill suited. A wider variety of mortgage payment arrangements is called for to answer the needs of first time home owners and of rental entrepreneurs in the future. To insure such mortgages against different risks requires more flexibility than is allowed under the act. More flexibility is required with regard to insurance premiums, mortgage terms, payment schedules and procedures for claim settlement, all of which impinge upon the ability of the corporation to fund and to act. I will have more to say about these on another occasion.
In summary, I would like to commend to the House and to the people of Canada the plan offered by the minister last evening which will assist Canadians to cope with the problems associated with renewing mortgages at high rates of interest. The mortgage plan meets the essential requirements. First, it gives help to those who need it most. It gives people the amount of help they need to get them through the difficult times. It does all of this fairly and without adding to inflationary pressures through excessive and indiscriminate expenditure of public resources.
I would like to remind hon. members and the country that mortgage renewal problems, distressing as they are, are not the only housing issues we have to confront. Tenants have problems, and I will be exploring solutions to those problems in my discussions beginning immediately with provincial housing ministers.
I had made reference to our efforts on behalf of the native people and the rural poor, and, as I have indicated, that program has a high place in my priorities as the minister reporting to this House and the government for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
We are concerned as well with the needs of a large proportion of the population; women raising children alone, the elderly and the handicapped who cannot fend for themselves in the marketplace. We have made important strides in broadening our social housing assistance and making it more acceptable. As a result, for example, of representations made by the provincial ministers at the conference earlier this year, and as a result of the efforts of the handicapped during this year, the corporation has taken steps to make more available to the handicapped increased access to our social programs. These efforts, I am sure, will be reflected not only in improved living conditions for many Canadians but also in an impetus to the housing industry and in the creation of a significant number of new jobs.
In concluding I would like to reiterate my comments on the effect of the measures the government is taking. They will deal
effectively and equitably with the problem of mortgage renewals. They will stimulate the production of rental housing, and, when combined with existing social housing programs, they will result in 40,000 rental units being supported by the government next year.
To achieve this, the government has allocated $150 million in direct expenditures next year for these initiatives, and a further $200 million has been allocated in the fiscal framework 1983-84 because of the special guarantee of interest deferral and other housing measures that may be required.
These figures are impressive, particularly given the over-all requirement for fiscal restraint, but they do not by themselves represent the full story. The federal government through its actions will cause a further $1.6 billion in private funds from the private sector to flow to the production of rental housing across Canada next year. This in turn will create jobs and will assist in improving the health of the residential building industry. I am not ashamed to say that this is done under a program which combines not only the government and the private sector, but the national government in co-operation with provincial and local governments and the private sector. They are co-operating in achieving these housing needs for Canadians.
We are all aware as well of the spin-offs from this massive investment; the multiplier effects the industry creates in other areas such as in home furnishings and in the appliance industry, all of which are presently in need of this stimulation.
The task remaining is for the House to translate the very obvious concern, which is taken for granted, and the expression of that concern from all sides of the House during the last few months, into action to assist Canadians who are being affected at this time because of high interest rates.
As I indicated, I will table a bill to amend the National Housing Act. The legislation is important. It will enable the government and Parliament to assist householders in renewing their mortgages through the mortgage renewal plan. It will enable the government and Parliament to assist first-time home buyers through modifications to the mortgage instrument, which, as I have indicated, are not now available in the present legislation. It will enable an additional stimulus to be provided to rental production by allowing CMHC to insure higher loan amounts on rental production. This demonstrates the interface of government with the private sector to the benefit of all Canadians.
I trust and pray that, just as my confidence in the government was vindicated by the government, so too will my confidence in the good sense of all hon. members of this House be vindicated by the speedy passage of this legislation, legislation which, as we all know, is sorely needed by Canadians at this time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words on the amendment on entering this debate are spoken in terms of sorrow because I realize what has happened in these last few weeks. We have had a minister of the Crown, obviously sincere and obviously trying his level
November 13, 1981

best to grapple with the problems of housing, suddenly catching the can and having to take responsibility for fundamental policies of the government which have nothing to do with finding the solution to the real problems in Canada. I am very sorry that a fine, new Member of Parliament should have to undergo this. He wrote off his right to pity. I know, when he stood up and, in his opening remarks today, said: "I praise the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) for doing this to me; I am pulling the spear into my own chest." I do fee! deeply sorry for any human being who has to carry the can on this particular isue.
What we are debating here is not just a budget. What we are debating here, in plain, blunt terms, is interest rates. We are suffering in a prison of myths started 40 years ago and carried on today by a small group of monetary and fiscal experts who have learned nothing in the last 40 years and have forgotten nothing. This whole debate hinges on the understanding we as Members of Parliament have of the use of interest rates. In the view of these experts, interest rates represent a tool of monetary policy, when in fact interest rates cause inflation. They look at interest rates as a tool to fight inflation when the truth is that interest rates cause inflation. That has shown up dramatically in the last eight or nine months with the housing industry and people who own homes being in the front lines. It has shown up dramatically in small businesses, and it has shown up in a dramatic way in big business, including great companies like General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson, John Deere and a whole assortment of companies which operate on the technique of credit for production, for inventory and for distribution. The interest rate load has passed the boundary of economics, over the abyss and into the mess we are in today. This puts into perspective what this debate is about. Normally it is the budget. We have listened to our spokesman for the Conservative Party-who is another new member and who is equally sincere and who is trying to do his best to put into words what he felt should have been done in this budget. I think it was a credible effort for the first time he has engaged in the opening part of a budget debate. What he was trying to say, Mr. Speaker, was that the missing ingredient in this budget, during this economic cycle, was the primary objective of developing this country. Developing this country would not cause inflation. If we bring together our unused plant capacity and our unused labour supply with the great supply of cash we have in Canada through our savings programs, these great challenges which face us economically can become great opportunities. That is what the spokesman for the Conservative Party was saying.
The speech by the representative from the New Democratic Party was a demonstration of what a master of words can do in ripping a helpless government apart. The irony of it all is that this is the man who helped get this government into power. He helped to defeat a budget in 1979 which had some of the provisions which should have been in this budget. I could not help but think of the irony of it as I listened to his
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
razor-edged remarks, cutting the heart out of the government members. He was one of the leaders in the movement to force the alliance between the NDP and the Liberals, who only had one objective, to get the Conservatives out of power. The good Lord, in His wisdom, is today dealing with these people in His own way.
This budget can be analysed very simply by asking yourself four or five questions. Did this budget provide a series of tax reductions for the things people need, want and would accept? Would this create a number of jobs which, in turn, would create a greater amount of tax revenue and help the government balance its budget over the next two or three years? Were there any tax reductions in this budget which met that criteria? There were six or seven of them in the Crosbie budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) had so much sport with over the last two years. It is a case of one island guy buzzing another island guy. Was there any proposal in this budget to reduce taxes to get the economy moving and help the Minister of Finance balance his budget over the next couple of years? The answer is, yes, there was one. That one provision is for a reduction of gross taxes on income from that horrible high level of 64 per cent in Ontario and most of the rest of Canada down to 50 per cent. The maximum income tax of an individual in Canada, both provincial and federal, is 50 per cent. That is all the government will now take away from you, instead of the outrageous 64 per cent.
There was an editorial in The Globe and Mail this morning which stated that there are only 50,000 people in this bracket who will benefit, and I think that most of them read The Globe and Mail. Do we in our party say that this provision is bad? The answer is, no, because whether you like this provision or not, these 50,000 people who will benefit quite extensively- they already have a Cadillac and a house which is paid for, so they cannot spend much more-will put their money back in the investment field because they are the type of people who will do this. They are the ones who hopefully will create the jobs, and the record shows that they always do. This party, through the words of every member who speaks, will support this part of the budget and this, of course, is where we differ from the NDP. They want the tax raised higher on these 50,000 people who make $100,000 a year. They are against any person having that kind of income. They believe we should all be down at the same level in an egalitarian society where there is no ownership of property. That was clearly stated by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party.
I repeat that this budget does make one provision for tax reduction. However, if we review the Crosbie budget, we will note that there was a proposal to deduct interest on mortgages, a proposal to deduct property tax for home owners-the renter already has that type of thing. This was proposed in the Crosbie budget, and the Liberals and the New Democratic Party turned it down. The Crosbie budget proposed an energy tax credit wherein any person who made less than $22,000 a

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
year was not taxed at all on energy. This allegiance of Tweedledum and Tweedledee now results in taxing oil and gas and everything else. Gas is up by 36 cents to 46 cents a gallon. That is a measurement of what the present budget shows when compared with the Crosbie budget.
What I am suggesting, following the lead of the spokesman for the Conservative Party, is that there should have been a vast series of tax reductions in the budget, tax reductions for any person who would invest as an individual in ownership of this country, for any person who would invest in pipelines into the north, for any persons investing in a power grid from the Yukon through to the Hamilton River-now called the Churchill-tying up the great energy resources of coal to use thermal heat, the great power grid which made all this energy available across the country. I would like to have seen tax reductions to encourage the development of a system to move hydrogen across the country in a way similar to oil, gas or electricity. There was a task force report from all parties in the House which recommended this as a number one priority. The system of moving hydrogen is much the same as for moving gas except it requires twice the pressure.
I could go on and list a number of projects. We have the prairies which are full of great natural river basins which have been empty for millions of years. We have the facilities now available to store water in those great basins. This water could be transported across the prairies to make industrial development available at a lower cost than in any other country in the world, particularly in the petrochemical industry. I would like to see that water go back to its original channel from the prairies right through to Ontario and right across the northwest of Ontario where is used to run. It can be done. I would like to see a development on the east coast to take advantage of these tremendous iron reserves we have in Labrador and around Ungava. I would like to see a tremendous development in the Hudson Bay area on the Nastapoka Islands and the Belchers, where iron is 70 per cent, tied into the big industrial complex we have around the Great Lakes where there are millions of people. We could produce steel even cheaper than we do today, and our steel is the cheapest in the world.
I can see one project after the other-with the economics all worked out-that could have been started in this budget. We could have put our men to work, and people tell me that would not be a policy of restraint! Whenever you spend money to make money, that does not cause inflation. That is the only way to fight inflation. That money can be spent on potential things or on immediate things.
I have before me a chart covering the years 1953 to 1981, and what it is is the pulse rate of the nation. It shows the pulse beating at different rates for nearly 30 years, and as that pulse rate is beating, we can see the country growing or taking sudden drops. As I look at the last 30 years on this chart I see a drop on the chart as a result of the budget of Walter Harris
in 1956. He used the same opening philosophy the minister used last night. I see a drop in 1959 under Donald Fleming. He made his budget presentation from the same seat occupied by the present minister. I remember that budget, and I remember how that policy was changed shortly afterward and how growth increased steadily for nine years without a break. Even when Walter Gordon brought in his budget, that made only a small tremor. Then there was the budget of Benson of 1968. We were going to wrestle inflation to the ground, but that budget sent us right down in one of the steepest drops we have ever had in our economic history. Once the country gathered itself together and fought its way up out of that, along came the 1974 budget of John Turner, after which there was a real drop. That was the time he double taxed by making the taxes of the provinces on the resource industries non-deductible. This country has never quite recovered from that double taxation of the mining and resource industries in the Turner budget of 1974. We have had stagflation ever since. Along with the United States, our country has been struggling to get going. All of a sudden we have this new budget. We are already into a recession and, instead of trying to do what the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), the spokesman for the Conservative Party, was saying, instead of trying to get outselves going, instead of getting up and taking advantage of the fact that there are men and women who need jobs and that there is lots of money available, if the tax rate is right, and instead of taking advantage of these great opportunities, the minister walked in here and repeated the same mistakes Walter Harris made in 1956, Fleming made in 1959, Benson made in 1968 and Turner made in 1974. The minister has turned this country downhill at high speed, with all the human suffering and frustration which will result.
We will get out of it, all right. This country is too strong even for politicians to push it around, but it is an unhappy time for me to go through this.
I say that this budget could be tested by three, four or five questions. I mentioned tax reductions, not just to please voters but to balance the budget by making more money available. That is a potential thing. I mentioned that the Crosbie budget had six or seven, and I will put on the record once again a reference to a special issue of "The Public Interest" in 1980. The article to which I refer is entitled "The Dissolution of the Keynesian Consensus", and it was written by James W. Dean. The article says:
On December 13, 1979, the government of Canada fell. For just six months the Conservatives had governed with a parliamentary minority, and they were defeated on a vote of no confidence. The issue was their first budget-a budget that rejected Keynesian economic policies, replacing them with radically different recommendations. Unemployment and slow growth were to be fought not by increasing the federal deficit but by reducing it.
This was a turnabout in what the Conservatives themselves had recommended when sitting in opposition just the year before. Their turnabout mirrored that of much of the economics profession throughout the English-speaking world. It was the decade's last dramatic reflection of a dissolving Keynesian consensus. This paper traces how that dissolution came about.
I put that on the record again to show that the intellectuals of the world recognized the significance of the Crosbie budget, even though we in Parliament did not at the time. It was the
November 13, 1981

first budget in the western world that deliberately tried to balance the budget by reducing taxes, and that is what the record will show over the centuries to come. One page of this morning's Globe and Mail was set aside for the federal budget. It says, "Little new spending in development strategy for the eighties." As The Globe and Mail read the development paper-and I read it too-The Globe and Mail does not see any new spending to make money in development in the whole decade to come.
The government had a great opportunity to pick this country up and to get it off this mythology of Keynes whereby the government frightens us with myths and bogey men that do not exist. One of the myths is that deficits are always inflationary. I have heard that for 25 years around here, and I simply say that deficits are not inflationary if the money is spent in productive enterprises. Deficits are not inflationary if the money is spent to make money. Deficits are not inflationary if the capacity of the industrial segment is available. Deficits are not inflationary if labour is available.
Surely the quantative evidence of the last 30 years should be listened to. More embarrassing still is another myth with which the government tries to frighten us, and that is that we have to have high interest rates in Canada so that money will not flow out. What a myth! Hon. members should look at the figures. Using just the number 2 to represent the total figure, in the last decade we sent out roughly $2 a year. What did we do last year after interest rates went up out of sight? Our export of capital went up from 2 to 10. If we were to add "billion" we would not be far out. High interest rates are supposed to draw money in, but the more we have raised interest rates in Canada, the more money has gone out-five times more.
I simply say that this budget fails in almost every test. I have not mentioned the transfer of social costs back to the provinces. Nor have I mentioned the question of indexing of income which is being done for one more year.
I want to conclude by stating those things in the budget that really hurt. I refer in particular to the minister in charge of housing, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and any resource minister. The final question we should ask ourselves is, where are their precise policies to reduce interest rates on the fiscal side? The answer is just the opposite.
The poor housing policy just announced by the minister is simply putting off the problem of interest rates. They call it deferring it, which means adding it to your debt. Instead of paying it out over 25 or 30 years, it will be paying it out over 35 or 40 years. It is a life sentence. That is what it means.
The answer should have been what was proposed to the minister in the House last spring from this side. We should have applied the same principle of the small business development bond to several fiscal fields. If a person wanted to lend money for housing, the export industry, farming or any other
The Budget-Mr. Breau
form of activity which is productive, that person should not be charged tax on his income. He could then afford to lend his money to the productive industries at roughly 8 to 10 per cent and not be behind in the game. The government naturally would not allow the fellow who received that money to use his interest payments as deductions. Therefore, it is a fair balance.
That principle could have been applied to housing. Now with interest rates bouncing around 16 and 17 per cent, and they will soon be down to 13 and 14 per cent because the market is forcing them down, not the theorists, a man could borrow the money for half the rate plus one. No army of civil servants would be required. Let the Farm Credit Corporation and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation be the agencies to handle that requirement. Whatever route you work with, this could have applied to vast segments of our economy where there is a human need as well as an economic need.
These directions for industries related to homes, farms, the export business and small business would be able to make enough profit and expand to produce the jobs which are the big human need in Canada today.
When everyone is making money, the tax collector makes money. He will get back three times over what was put out originally. The tax collector would be the big beneficiary, but everyone would benefit. It would not be a case of one side winning and one side losing, what they call the zero sum society. It would be a modern society of common sense where everybody wins because everybody is participating in the common goal.
These proposals were all made by members on this side last spring. I thought the minister was listening. He spoke favourably of it. I thought the Minister of Agriculture was listening because he went out and talked the same. However, this budget has now cut the throats of these two ministers. They are destroyed. The man who really should be destroyed is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who did not defend those two ministers in front of his own Minister of Finance, making certain that they were protected by carrying out in the budget what was promised to the people before this budget was laid down.
I wish there was another name in the amendment which the Conservative Party has moved. We are getting the guy who has to get the blame, but I think it is the wrong person. I want to conclude by saying in one sentence something I said before. This budget is not only wrong for this time of the cycle in Canada, it is a fraud on the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this important budget debate now being held in the House. First of all, I would like to mention that during the past year, I was involved in two special committees of the House, one on North-South relations and the other on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements. I am glad to see that the government has made a thorough study of the two reports tabled by these two task forces and that both reports received the unanimous approval of all parties in the House, that is, of

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Breau
the parties of the members sitting on these committees, and that the government has accepted the general principles and orientation of the two committees.

I am happy to see the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) in the chamber this afternoon. He was a very active member of the task force on North-South relations which I had the honour to chair. He was of great help in that process, as were all members of that task force.
I believe we have helped in the process of reform of this place which is so important to influencing government policy and giving a philosophical framework to the government, both in North-South and in fiscal arrangements. That will be very helpful to the government and the country. I mention that because on both issues we have a reaffirmation of the government's commitment, first to North-South relations and the development assistance budget of the government and also in the area of fiscal arrangements.

I was very happy to read in the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) last night, that the government is now making concrete proposals on the renewal of fiscal arrangements for the period from 1982 to 1987.1 find it gratifying to see the extent to which the minister used the report of the Parliamentary Task Force on Fiscal Arrangements in preparing the federal government's proposals. In fact, it can be said that basically, the federal proposals are in line with our own recommendations. The federal proposal is concerned with three distinct aspects of fiscal arrangements, that is, equalization payments, established programs financing and fiscal rationalization. This is more or less the order used by our task force in its report.
The conceptual framework we used, which may be found in chapter 2 of the report, identifies four basic elements with respect to the future of fiscal arrangements, that is, sharing of tax revenue by the two levels of government, economic and fiscal co-ordination, fiscal equalization and financing of provincial programs that are in the national interest. And here I am thinking more specifically of hospital care, medicare and the Canada Assistance Plan. Although the latter is not one of the programs identified under the EPF program, it is still a very important social program in our country.
To have an overview of the fiscal reality in our federal system, one must situate intergovernmental transfer payments such as equalization and EPF payments within the context of the public finances of each level of government. Since 1957, the federal government has more than quadrupled the fiscal space available to the provinces where personal income tax is concerned through the use of tax point transfers, which has enabled the provinces to finance their expenditures on health and education. The provinces have therefore received a larger share of the country's public revenue, and also more flexibility, because with the tax point system, the province is free to apply
or appropriate these public funds as it sees fit. The provinces have become stronger financially compared to the federal government.
From 1959 to 1979, the federal share of public revenue fell from over 58 per cent to less than 46 per cent, while the share of provinces and municipalities rose from 42 per cent to 54 per cent. If one subtracts federal transfer payments and considers them as provincial revenue, one sees that the federal government's share of revenue, which was 52 per cent in 1959, is now less than 34 per cent of what it was in 1979. These figures tell us a great deal, Mr. Speaker, in fact they indicate that from the fiscal point of view, Canada is probably the most decentralized federation in the world, despite the fact that it is said that the federal government, especially under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), has been a centralizing government. Not, however, Mr. Speaker, if we look, at the figures which show that since 1959, the share of total public revenue in Canada spent by the federal government dropped from 52 per cent to 34 per cent.
Therefore, on the basis of those facts a majority of members of the parliamentary task force on tax agreements concluded that it would be unwise to proceed with new transfers of income tax points as suggested by some provinces. Such transfers would indeed reduce the means available to the federal government to make sure that provincial involvement in areas such as health and post-secondary education are consistent with the achievement of major national objectives. Should some tax fields be taken away from the federal government, it would be unable to govern in the interests of all the people. In addition, new transfers of income tax points would reduce the capacity of the federal government to manage the economy and would favour the wealthiest provinces where the value of tax points is higher.
The government proposals to renew tax agreements do not provide for any new transfer of tax points and thus they entirely agree with the conclusions of the task force in connection with the sharing of tax revenues between the two levels of government. It should also be noted that neither the Minister of Finance nor the task force suggest a reduction in the tax fields granted to the provinces in the past two years. For example, tax fields granted to the provinces in 1977 cannot be patriated.
As concerns economic and fiscal co-ordination, the task force recommended that the federal government maintain the tax agreements while still requiring that they be subjected to the three principles outlined by the Minister of Finance in December, 1980. These principles relate to the administrative practicability of tax measures, the uniformity of the direct tax base and the avoidance of fiscal obstacles to the flow of capital between provinces. We also suggested the development of a fiscal behaviour code which, without preventing the federal government from stimulating economic development in have-not regions, would subject all governments in Canada to a
November 13, 1981

certain fiscal discipline. We also suggested the establishment of a federal-provincial committee of officials which would report periodically to the Minister of Finance on the state of the economic union. This committee would look into various matters of fiscal harmonization between the different governments and could consider drafting an economic behaviour code on taxation, spending and economic regulatory processes. The Minister of Finance's proposals on fiscal harmonization are very important, Mr. Speaker, because it is essential to maintain in Canada the principles outlined by the minister himself at the 1980 finance minister's conference. He proposes consultations with all the provinces, including those not included in the tax arrangements, to look into matters of fiscal harmonization and develop corrective mechanisms if need be.
This issue of fiscal harmonization scares many people because it is very complex, Mr. Speaker.
