But without any fiscal harmonization or co-ordination to ensure that all levels of government in Canada, both federal and provincial, will act likewise when the time comes to collect new taxes or to legislate in this area, there would be a tremendous jungle in Canada. What would happen is that the provinces would compete against each other for taxes and, as a result, someone who did not want to pay any taxes would not pay any anywhere in Canada. I am therefore pleased that the minister has accepted this recommendation of the task force on fiscal arrangements. The members of our task force can only be pleased with the minister's proposals because they are clearly made in the same spirit as our report.
We analysed very thoroughly the question of fiscal equalization. We made some important recommendations. That topic formed the highlight of our report. It is worth noting that members of this House, or members of a committee of this House from different political parties, are able to speak with one voice on the question of equalization, as this is the issue. Canada could not exist as it exists today without the concept and philosophy of providing an equality of fiscal capacity up to the national average for every province of this country. How could the provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia or my own province of New Brunswick, for example, provide the degree of social services they provide to their citizens without equalization? Without it we would have two or three levels of Canadians. That would be intolerable in this country. We proposed that the program continue as an unconditional transfer of resources to provinces that are below the national average in fiscal capacity per capita. We also said that a program of equalization which would measure the fiscal capacity was the best way to arrive at this objective of equality or of comparable services from one part of the country to the other.
With regard to the treatment of natural resources, we could not make precise recommendations because, at the time we reported, there had not been an oil and gas pricing agreement
The Budget-Mr. Breau
with Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. However, we recommended that decisions taken in regard to this question should be inspired by certain principles that we considered important. First, the receipts from natural resources should only be included in the equalization formula to the extent that they serve to finance what can be considered normal provincial services; second, that no special category of receipts or benefits from natural resources be excluded from the equalization formula, and that all receipts of this kind be included in the formula that established the entitlement to the have-not provinces; and third, it was important to have some kind of ceiling on the proportion of equalization entitlement to either the gross national product or to some other ceiling to protect the integrity of the federal treasury. It should be noted that many people do not recognize this need. I was struck, when listening to the debate in the House and travelling across the country with the task force, by the extent to which people do not realize that while equalization payments to provinces are calculated on the taxing capacity of all provinces, but influenced mainly by the rich provinces, all payments come out of the federal treasury. It is a unique program because it indicates that automatically, without questions asked and without regard to the moneys coming into the federal treasury, on the basis of the fiscal capacity of provincial governments taking 29 tax fields, the federal treasury should pay this out. It is a unique system. On the question of equalization it indicates that the capacity of the federal treasury at any given time should not be a factor which would deprive the have-not provinces of achieving an average fiscal capacity per capital It is important to note that. We said it was an important principle. However, while it is pegged to provincial taxes or what happens in the provincial field, there should be some kind of ceiling to protect the federal treasury.
The task force considered that it was normal that the approach selected to deal with revenue from natural resources would result in a substantial reduction in equalization payments now being made on the basis of such revenue and that, as a result, Ontario's eligibility for equalization payments would be postponed for at least a few years. We also recommended abrogating the special provision on personal income, as a result of which Ontario is now excluded from equalization payments.
Those were thus the main recommendations of the task force. They are similar to the proposals of the Minister of Finance, because the minister, while wishing to retain the representative taxation system, proposes to change the present formula by broadening the fiscal capability measure on which it is based, and by setting Ontario's fiscal productivity as the norm for equalization payments. In addition, the Minister of Finance is proposing that municipal and local taxes should all be included in the equalization formula in order to determine the size of the payment to provinces receiving equalization.

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Breau

I believe that adopting the Ontario standard as the minister proposed in the budget is equitable and fair. It prevents us from adopting the special discriminatory procedures or positions that we had last year to protect the federal treasury from a rampant increase in equalization payments because of something happening, for example, in the resource field. I believe that adopting the Ontario standard is fair. Considering that the decisions on levels of municipal taxation in Ontario are not in the hands of a single government but in the hands of an array of municipal governments, I believe it will turn out to be very generous for provinces that are recipients of equalization payments.

Concerning established programs financing, we made a number of very elaborate recommendations. These recommendations deal with the terms and conditions of established programs as well as their financing. On the terms and conditions of health programs, the task force recommended that after consulting with the provincial governments, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) establish clear health program conditions based on explicit criteria allowing their implementation to be monitored. We also recommended, in respect of the Minister of National Health and Welfare as well as the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) and any other minister designated by the government, that there be an annual report to Parliament on the state of programs or on what the minister refers to as "national standards".
A comparison of the task force's recommendations in the areas of health care and post-secondary education show a striking similarity. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) proposes that national health care standards be clarified and that an efficient mechanism be set up in consultation with the provinces to ensure that they be adhered to. Concerning post-secondary education, the minister proposes that new arrangements be worked out in consultation with the provinces, and in view of the fact that the minister asked for different treatment in cases where there is no post-secondary education agreement, it can be seen that the minister is getting near to our recommendation to separate the two, and hopefully in the course of these negotiations with the provinces, the Canadian government will show fairness in the areas of health care and post-secondary education in order that we have not only an agreement on the conditions of those programs, particularly on the matter of extra billing by physicians, but also an agreement on post-secondary education national goals and an agreement on the implementation of those programs and the way these terms and conditions will be interpreted in the future, because currently there is not even agreement on the interpretation.
On the issue of established programs financing, especially the federal contribution to health care and post-secondary education programs, and the treatment of part of the financing
transfer concerning established programs, the budget proposes that it be abolished in the interest of restraint.
Mr. Speaker, it must be said that it was not quite what the task force recommended, but what did matter to its members was that there be-and this is my own interpretation-no real basic reduction from one year to the next. With respect to the growth of the federal contribution, as well as of the expenditures, that is to say in the programs administered by the provinces we agree that in the future adjustments may be made.
I am glad to see that the government has accepted that recommendation of the task force, namely to maintain the level of financing, because, as the minister said during today's oral questions period, although the elimination of the system of revenue guarantee will cost $914 million to the provinces in 1982-83, we must keep in mind that when the minister proposes to close the loopholes-

The minister proposed to close the loopholes in the tax expenditure accounts. This will have the effect of increasing the federal tax base or the basic federal tax. All provinces except Quebec use the federal tax base to establish their own provincial income taxes. They are a percentage of the federal tax. While this will cost the provinces $914 million in 1982-83 they will receive, because of the changes, $1,083 million more in 1982-83. They will receive more in this current year, or approximately $47 million. While the net effect will be a loss starting in 1983-84, in the aggregate for the next two fiscal years the provinces will not lose one cent from the elimination of the revenue guarantee.
One must say that the revenue guarantee is a very inequitable form of fiscal transfer. I can see that the revenue guarantee was necessary in 1972 to protect provinces against sudden changes in the federal tax base because of tax reform, but the provinces have had ten years to adapt their provincial tax rates. We must not forget that the revenue guarantee is one point of personal income tax and the rest is cash. It is very inequitable toward poor provinces. It provides more of a guarantee to the rich provinces than to the poor ones. I think the way the government is dealing with this is in the spirit of the task force report. It does not effectively reduce in the aggregate in the next two years the amount of money the provinces will receive from the federal government when we take into account the moneys they will have because of the changes to the federal tax base. It will not be redressed. There will be no $1.5 billion cut in the next two years. I see the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) smile. The only reduction will be $1.9 billion out of total transfers of $104 billion over five years. When one considers the changes to equalization, bringing in the municipal taxes at the Ontario level, I am sure that in the case of the have-not provinces at least, there will be no reduction at all, even when the elimination of the revenue guarantee is considered.
November 13, 1981

I am waiting for the cash flow figures on the changes to equalization. If we look at the budget document entitled "Fiscal Arrangements in the Eighties" which was tabled last evening by the Minister of Finance we will see on page 45 that the estimates of equalization of payments under the proposed formula will go from $4.5 billion in 1982-83 to over $7 billion by 1986-87. There will be very generous increases, and it is estimated that the average annual rate of growth of equalization payments will be 11.4 per cent.
The elimination of the revenue guarantee, accompanied by an increase in the federal tax base, and the elimination of the tax loopholes that the minister proposed will bring more equity into the system, and the have-not provinces will be protected by an enriched equalization system because their tax capacity will be equalized after bringing in municipal taxes to the Ontario level.
Everyone knows that municipal taxes in Ontario are very high. In Newfoundland there are practically none; in New Brunswick they are very low; in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island they are way below the national average. The result will be that municipal taxes in the poor provinces will be way down compared with the national average, while in Ontario they will be way up. There will be a more generous equalization payment to the have-not provinces.
We must not consider just one proposal of the budget in isolation from all the others. The piinister is proposing a more generous, equitable and just equalization system that will protect the poor provinces-I do not like the word poor so I should say the have-not provinces although in some cases they are richer than the others. Quebec and the others will be protected because the municipal taxes in Quebec are a lot lower than they are in Ontario. Quebec decided to structure its finances differently and increase school taxes, so property taxes there are lower than those in Ontario. By doing that, we eliminate a very inequitable form of fiscal transfer that was an automatic, unconditional transfer to the rich provinces as well as to the poor ones. Over the last quarter of a century we have established that the only unconditional payment to the provinces should be the equalization program. That is a different kind of program.
The rich provinces need money but they do not need it at a time when the federal government is in debt and has to pay 20 per cent of its budget for debt charges. The federal government not only has to look after things that come under federal jurisdiction, such as fisheries, defence, international development, foreign affairs, energy and transportation, but it must always keep in mind the dangers of developing what the Minister of Finance called last April "fiscal dualism". This is the case where rich provinces get richer and poorer provinces get poorer. That has to be a concern of the federal Parliament and that is why the elimination of the revenue guarantee, coupled with a very enriched equalization program to the Ontario standard with municipal taxes, will mean we will have a more fair system to protect have-not provinces and thereby have a better federation.
The Budget-Mr. Vankoughnet

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when many feel we are sliding into a deepening recession, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), instead of delivering an equitable budget, has presented much gloss and little substance as a prelude to his potential leadership of the Liberal Party.
Many Canadians may not think they are in for tax increases and they may be thankful for small mercies, but they should be made aware of the fact that the present Liberal government has once again shown little mercy by neglecting the serious economic problems facing Canadians today. This budget is merely a manipulation of wealth and very little else.
Once again we have here a budget which gives the impression that the government does not know what to do about the economy of Canada. Incredible expenditures have allowed pork-barrelling and the socialization of private enterprise. This represents the worst in public spending while it continues to discourage Canadians from investing in the future of this great land, with confidence.
This government that masquerades as a Liberal government is trapped in its own snare. After a decade of depending on Gallup polls for economic decisions and governing by them, it finds itself out of band-aids, as have other socialist regimes throughout the world.
There is no question that our economic problems can only be solved by common sense. The government has failed to do this. Canadians desperately want a definite sense of direction and a policy designed to restore confidence in our economy. We desperately need public policies which will achieve sound economic growth, improved opportunities for employment, and a climate of competitive free enterprise, and which will encourage Canadians to work and invest.
Canada is a country with enormous potential yet the government is failing miserably, in the economic policies put forward in this budget, to maximize the opportunities that face us. Hard-working Canadians have become frustrated with the widening gap between our known potential and the current uncertain economic reality. The federal government's high interest rates and high inflation is ruining individuals, such as farmers, businessmen, and home owners across this land.
There is no question that our priorities must be to reduce inflation and interest rates. The question is whether we should continue to follow the policies of this government which have caused the problems we now have. Because of these policies, we are now experiencing the worst inflation recorded in Canada since the end of wartime price controls. Throughout 1981 inflation has been in double digits, which in turn increased interest rates to unacceptably high levels. This situation discourages potential growth in this country and uncertainty discourages long-term capital projects.
Businessmen and farmers cannot operate under increasing debt repayment schedules. Home owners are losing their homes because of huge mortgage renewal increases. Through no fault of their own, hard-working Canadians face extraordi-

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Vankoughnet
nary circumstances, all because of this and former Liberal policies.
The government is only paying lip service to reducing government deficits and reducing the inflationary pressures in the economy. The past spending policies to which this government is bound prevent it from effectively attacking inflation and high interest rates in an effort to change our destructive economic and social direction.
This trap, which is in evidence today in the demise of provincial government representation will either destroy Canada or the so-called Liberal party. The federal deficit has climbed to over $12 billion in the 1981-82 fiscal year.
Further confiscation and socialization under the catchy term "Canadianization" is undesirable and is wrong for our economy. Increased taxation as a means of improving a deficit caused by mismanagement is the wrong approach. New taxes on top of those imposed under the recent energy agreements will have a negative impact on risk-taking and investment.
Government restraint can be achieved only if genuine efforts are made to control public spending at the federal level if it does not renege on obligations to the provinces and local governments through transfer payment cuts.
It is politically popular to create new expectations for new programs, but people are now realizing that ultimately they pay dearly for these administrative jungles. These programs are expensive, and the money would be better left in the hands of Canadians rather than having Big Brother do it for them. Programs which are introduced must be assessed very carefully to determine if they are affordable now and in the future. The only way to ensure future affordability is to encourage a productive and growing economy which would in turn generate needed financial support.
The reduction of interest rates in the United States will benefit Canadians; but without government action here, a proper climate will not be achieved. Productivity will play an important role in raising our living standards, if given proper incentives. Co-operation in providing programs and incentives to train workers for new opportunities should be given a high priority. If we had trained people for new developments in such sectors as energy production, high technology products, biotechnology and the use of computers, it would greatly add to Canada's economic growth. Duplication and competition in the training of individuals should be avoided, and co-operation with the provinces should be a priority.
There is a need for government to ensure that the personal taxation system is designed to encourage effort, saving and investment. It has to be clear that government supports those people who are willing to devote their efforts and resources to helping Canada reach its potential. We should be neutralizing inequities in the taxation of capital gains, and providing a greater incentive to undertake necessary risk. It is wrong and makes little sense to tax gains which are solely attributable to inflation.
The business community must be given incentives for increased investment without government interference. Foreign investment, capital and expertise are needed for economic development over the next decade. Responsible foreign investment has built this nation and could continue to strengthen it if foreign investors are treated in a fair and forthright manner. Tariffs will continue to fall as a result of the latest GATT arrangements. Competition from low-wage countries and trading blocs is also intensifying. Over-regulation of private enterprise in Canada is just too burdensome. More than ever we need a new national economic strategy to combat inflation and encourage productivity and investment.
The lost time the federal government undertook to reach an energy pricing and revenue-sharing agreement with the oil and gas producing provinces has increased Canada's imports of oil, reduced international confidence in the economy and put downward pressure on the dollar, which is a major cause of double-digit inflation. The inability to deal with strikes such as that of the postal workers and grain handlers has contributed to a lower confidence in the Canadian economy. It is easier for politicians to grant increased social benefits without taxation than to pay as one goes. The fact is that people still pay. It is a well understood fact that the cause of inflation is irresponsible government spending which exceeds the real worth of production and services. The problem is therefore political.
Some 900,000 Canadians need jobs now and for the future. There is a strong need for a comprehensive Canadian industrial strategy in order to make the best use of our abundant supply of resources for the future. We need made-in-Canada solutions to made-in-Canada problems, many which were created by years of indifferent Liberal governments. Canadians need support and encouragement to lift them out of the consumer gloom and away from the negative effects of recession. Canada's potential for success is immense, and the government once again fails to take effective steps to get the Canadian economy moving.
If in fact we are slipping into a recession, as many think we are, then the federal government must stand up to this and not run away from its responsibility, because the same federal government got us into this through years of economic mismanagement. Government spending has been irresponsible, excessive and inflationary. This situation must be curbed so that we do not saddle further generations with unbearable debt built up over the years.
There are many problems here in Canada to be solved before we look for others to take on at the taxpayers' expense. Efforts must be made at home to strengthen the Canadian economy and the Canadian dollar. Before the government gives advice to others, it should prove that it is in a position of credibility by righting the economic wrongs of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Canadian taxpayers deserve no less. In the fast paced world, we must keep up if we are to remain competitive. The need for post-secondary education and

research and development is imperative now and for a strong future, and the government must ensure their continuing importance through active support and encouragement.
The federal government has taken Canada from the third highest standard of living in the world in 1968, to the thirteenth, in 1980. We have so many raw materials and energy that other countries with higher standards of living import that we wonder why Canada appears to be slipping when we should be near the top. The Canadian public wants answers and a solution, one which does not appear in yet another ineffective housekeeping Liberal budget. Real problems need real solutions. The problems have been known for some time now. Why are we not getting the solutions? The economy certainly needs help. Canadians need fundamental, straightforward, no-nonsense budgets to deal with the difficult times the Liberals have created.
The finance minister is using the huge sums of energy taxes to be collected by the federal government over the next five years to help reduce the inflationary deficit and curb excessive government spending, costing Canadians an average of $1400 per family per year. There is a need to combine long and short-term planning in the framework of a comprehensive industrial strategy for Canada. In the longer run, there is a need for government encouragement and assistance, training programs, research and development, promotion assistance, modernization of Canadian industry and improvement in our transportation systems. The government should help the private sector create new jobs and develop the market in Canadian expertise.
Experience shows that people respond to strong leadership which produces positive action rather than mere words or theories. A positive, enthusiastic attitude and environment results in more effort and more results from the same resources. Other countries have done this with fewer resources.
We in Canada have a great deal of potential; but we must believe in ourselves and follow a positive sense of direction to success. The government must take positive steps to build up the productive side of the economy and instil confidence in the marketplace. This is overdue, especially at this time when recent reports indicate consumer confidence in September of 1981 was at a 20-year low. Commercial bankruptcies were some 16 per cent higher in the first three quarters of 1981 than in the same period last year and 37 per cent higher than the same period two years ago. Farm bankruptcies were 133 per cent higher than in the first nine months of 1979. Inflation has pushed consumer prices in September of 1981 to 12.5 per cent higher than in September of 1980. Transportation costs are up 20.3 per cent. Housing costs are up 13.4 per cent. Fuel oil costs are up almost 55 per cent over the same time last year.
While wages are not keeping pace with inflation, consumers are falling behind. Even with the recent reduction by 1.5 per cent in the Canadian interest rates, they remain high in comparison with historic levels and in comparison with other major industrialized nations. The Canadian prime rate today is at some 18 per cent. Two years ago, the Canadian prime rate
The Budget-Mr. Vankoughnet
was at 14.75 per cent, while ten years ago it was 6.25 per cent. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate in October of 1981 was 8.3 per cent, the highest level in three years, with a record number of people out of work for the month of October. Last year's federal government deficit was a record $12.7 billion. The gross national debt is some $119 billion, which resulted in the expenditure of almost $11 billion last year just to service the government's debt. This amounts to almost one tax dollar in every four.
The measures announced by the government in its budget do not address the serious problems of high interest rates by taking positive action to combat them. Guaranteeing interest deferrals which are added to the struggling home owner's cost of housing in the long run does little to bring relief to Canadian home owners. This small token of assistance is of little comfort to both those eligible and those across the fine line who are not eligible for the assistance. They are faced by so many other economic hardships that anything other than an honest attempt at total economic encouragement does little to ease their burden. Canadians look for assistance with a view to a better future, not merely a deferral of the present plan with no economic improvement in sight.
The availability and affordability of housing are two serious problems in Canada and are largely the result of the government's high interest rate policy. Canada needs some 220,000 new housing units each year, but with shortfalls last year and predicted over this year and next this could result in a shortage of some 140,000 homes over the three-year period.
High interest rates have effectively ground apartment construction to a halt, resulting in a serious shortfall of rental accommodation in many areas of Canada. Tenants as well as home owners are hard hit by the current high rates of interest.
High mortgage rates are clearly having an impact on the affordability of housing in Canada. Over half a million Canadians will renew their mortgages this year. According to CMHC, 40,000 Canadian families will lose their homes because they cannot afford to renew their mortgages at current rates. The government must address itself to this serious problem facing Canadians.
Canadians may remember the Liberal promises in 1979 and 1980 that energy prices would stay low, and in particular that gasoline prices would rise by less than 14 cents a gallon in 1980. Depending on the location, gasoline prices in 1980 rose by between 22 cents and 29 cents a gallon, far in excess of the promised 14 cents. Since the election, the price of home heating fuel has risen by some 44 cents a gallon. It is estimated that by 1986 gasoline prices will climb to at least 80 cents a litre, or $3.60 a gallon in most provinces. Heating oil is estimated to go to 60 cents a litre, or $2.70 a gallon, and natural gas prices could double to some $10 a thousand cubic feet. So much for Liberal promises of cheaper energy.
The 18-month delay in reaching an energy pricing agreement caused the loss of tens of thousands of jobs and delayed the construction of two needed oil sands plants. The federal

November 13, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Vankoughnet government should take measures to ensure the oil industry is working again in an effort to keep jobs and exploration in Canada. As a result of the government's new increase in energy taxes, estimated at some $50 billion over the next five years, Canadians expect the government to direct these funds wisely.
There exists in this country today unacceptably high rates of unemployment, and yet at the same time we hear of serious shortages of certain critical skilled employees in Canada. Together with the strong need for a comprehensive economic and industrial policy for Canada to co-ordinate, plan and modernize its industries for the future, we see inadequate training and industrial policies and a lack of co-ordination among all levels of government and between the public and private sectors. We need a national employment and training plan to co-ordinate efforts to match skilled people to modern trades, and the federal government must contribute time, effort and funding to achieve this very important goal. If we are to keep industry in Canada, we must develop the technology and the training and co-ordinating programs and we must give encouragement to implement them and to modernize our industry for the future. There is a need for a strong effort at all levels to ensure we fill the important job shortages in skilled trades and preserve post-secondary education in Canada.
I have spoken in this House before about the need for a comprehensive industrial strategy for Canada and made specific reference to the need to ensure that the Canadian textile and clothing industry survives and grows so that we do not become dangerously dependent on a wide range of imports.
The federal government announced a new policy for Canada's textile and clothing industry on June 19, 1981, that reinforced investment confidence in this important industry which employs many Canadians directly and indirectly. Investors need confidence through long-term planning and stability to make the large-scale commitments necessary in high capital business today.
The policy as announced supported both assistance in modernizing viable firms in the textile and clothing industries and the provision of new employment in communities most vulnerable to foreign competition in these sectors, as the government intends to allow gradual increases of low-cost imports in the Canadian market.
In light of the October 26, 1981, press release from the Prime Minister's office, associated with the announcement of the members of the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, it is felt by some members of the textile and clothing industry that the context and thrust of this later release confuses the thrust of the textile policy announced last June 19. The later release indicates that the Government of Canada is committed to the promotion of a freer world trade environment by offering freer market access for foreign textile and clothing products.
The release goes on to indicate that while pursuing this policy the Canadian government fully intends to help affected industries, communities and workers adjust to the reality of a less protected domestic market, and that in order to smooth the transition the government will, among other things, establish a special assistance program.
The Canadian economy needs assistance and support if our industries are to survive and prosper. The government should make every effort to ensure that different sectors of our industries grow and compete, rather than say it does not think they can compete so it will offer them assistance to readjust. This is not the kind of positive attitude required to instil the confidence in the private sector necessary for the commitment to large scale infusions of time, capital and hard work necessary for survival and growth.
The government should see to it that its programs, both in theory and in practice, give Canadian industries support and encouragement when they need it most. Only then, when all is well at home, can the government honestly look elsewhere. We simply cannot afford to let our industries disappear through lack of effort or through intellectual theorizing when other countries in the world are doing their utmost to save their own industries. The federal government must promote Canada just as other countries so strongly promote their own interests. Canada would be in a better position to help others if she were strong herself.
The federal government should promote funds and energy toward a comprehensive industrial policy that promotes, preserves and improves Canadian industry so that Canada and Canadians grow stronger as a nation with a strong economy and all the good things that go along with it.
The federal government recently raised the Farm Credit Corporation's interest rate from 14 per cent to 16.75 per cent, thereby dealing Canadian farmers another heavy blow. There is a problem regarding the lack of adequate funding for the Farm Credit Corporation which has resulted in the Farm Credit Corporation running out of funds. The government must recognize that modern Canadian farming is dependent on credit. The current high levels of interest rates and lack of funding from the Farm Credit Corporation, combined with such soaring input costs as fuel and fertilizers are creating hardships for many farmers.
In conclusion I should like to emphasize that the Canadian people needed and expected a strong budget that would face
November 13, 1981

the current economic problems head on with responsible solutions. Once again, the government did not see fit to provide Canada with such a budget. Just as Liberal governments have disappeared at the provincial level, it does not appear long before that happens federally because the people of Canada cannot and will not stand for such further indifference and neglect from this Liberal government.
The Budget-Mr. Vankoughnet
